entries.title: Kyle Teel leaves White Sox game at Rangers with ankle injury
entries.summary: <p>ARLINGTON, Texas — Kyle Teel had to be helped off the field after suffering a left ankle injury in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a>’ series-opening victory Monday at Texas.</p><p>The second-year catcher, who missed most of the first three months of the season with hamstring and knee injuries, was in visible pain after diving to his left in an attempt to tag out Ezequiel Duran at home in the bottom of the second inning.</p><p>After the scoring play, Teel appeared unable to put any pressure on his left leg. The Sox said he was being evaluated.</p><p>Teel (.190/.271/.317, two homers, 14 RBI) had struggled at the plate <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/06/chicago-white-sox-catcher-kyle-teel-will-venable-home-runs-mlb-nationals-yankees-red-sox-triple-a-charlotte" target="_blank" ><u>since returning</u></a> from the injured list June 22, but provided the Sox a desperately needed defensive upgrade over Drew Romo, who replaced him Monday, and Edgar Quero, who has logged a .594 OPS the past month at Triple-A Charlotte.</p><p>Manager Will Venable, who helped his prized backstop off the field along with Sox trainer James Kruk, has called Teel arguably the Sox’ best player. Venable said over the weekend that Teel had just been “getting into his rhythm and into his form.”</p><p>Depending on the severity of Teel’s injury, it likely adds the catcher position to general manager Chris Getz’s wish list before the Aug. 3 trade deadline.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Texas.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>LM Otero/AP Photos</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Seeing double</b></h3><p>Sox batters smacked seven doubles off Rangers pitchers in their 10-3 win, including two from Miguel Vargas (two RBI) and a three-run double from Andrew Benintendi. </p><p>Munetaka Murakami lasered his two-bagger 107.5 mph to right field in the first inning against Jacob deGrom, which marked the rookie’s fourth hit since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/10/white-sox-activate-munetaka-murakami-from-injured-list-option-jacob-gonzalez-to-charlotte" target="_blank" ><u>returning from the IL</u></a> before the All-Star break.</p><p>Venable said he wasn't concerned about Murakami’s sluggish return, with 11 strikeouts in his first 27 plate appearances back with the Sox.</p><p>“The swing decisions are there,” Venable said. “There’s some balls that he probably has swung and missed at that he wants back, [ones] that we’re used to seeing those being hit really hard.”</p><p>Venable said he’s encouraged by a series of hard lineouts Murakami has hit the other way.</p><p>“Especially with left-handed hitters, when you see balls squared off to backside, to the opposite field, to me that’s a really good precursor to being able to drive the ball on the pull side,” Venable said. “Even when he’s not hitting homers, he’s making an impact.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div happy to come back to Arlington, Texas, where the former outfielder played for the Rangers in 2015, and where he returned as Bruce Bochy’s associate manager en route to their 2023 World Series title.</p><p>“Special place that I’ve had really good memories of, going back to being a player, getting traded over here,” Venable said in the dugout at Globe Life Field. “The one time I was in the playoffs as a player I was with this team.”</p><p>Rangers president Chris Young “is one of my best friends in life and one of the people that’s had the most impact on me in my life, and certainly my baseball career,” Venable said.</p><p>“There is so much that I learned from that World Series run, from those players, from Bruce Bochy, from Chris Young and Nick Hundley, who’s in the front office as well,” Venable said. “And then you’ve got to figure a lot of stuff out on your own.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Colson Montgomery’s All-Star snub firing him up for White Sox' second-half surge
entries.summary: <p>ARLINGTON, Texas — Colson Montgomery didn’t need another chip on his shoulder, but he’ll take it.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a>’ lanky shortstop has heard his whole career that he’s too big to stick at his position, that his hefty strikeout rate would keep him from being a viable big-leaguer and, entering this season, that his team wasn’t going anywhere.</p><p>Now, despite leading shortstops in home runs, Montgomery, 24, has been told he’s not an All-Star, giving him one more thing to prove people wrong about.</p><p>After launching out of the break in Toron-to with a double Friday that cleared the loaded bases and a timely home run Sunday — No.  24 in his second big-league season — Montgomery said his All-Star snub is motivating him in the second half, “as it should.”</p><p>“As a competitor, you should see yourself as the best, because if you don't, you're just selling yourself short,” he said before the Sox returned stateside for a three-game set with the Rangers. “You're not really giving yourself the inner confidence that you need to play this game, especially with how much it can just beat you down.”</p><p>That’s coming from somebody who knows it. Montgomery — who left Monday's game after fouling a ball off his shin and was considered day-to-day — took a mental beating at Triple-A to start last season, prompting Sox brass <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/28/colson-montgomery-white-sox-year-2" target="_blank" ><u>to pull him from game action altogether</u></a> to regroup at their Arizona training complex.</p><p>Since then, Montgomery has established himself one of baseball’s most productive shortstops at the plate while flashing more leather than the Sox could’ve expected.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Colson Montgomery goes deep! <a href="https://t.co/rEuUrBtC7V">pic.twitter.com/rEuUrBtC7V</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://x.com/whitesox/status/2078896606393295089?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 19, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>His two-run bomb at the Rogers Centre on Sunday was the 45th of his career, coming just a few days shy of a year since slugging <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/07/22/colson-montgomery-first-homer-white-sox-streak" target="_blank" ><u>his first career MLB home run</u></a> on July 22, 2025, at Tampa. Only Kyle Schwarber (57) and Junior Caminero (49) logged more dingers over that time, according to MLB statistician Sarah Langs.</p><p>Montgomery’s work before the break still wasn’t enough to get him an All-Star nod <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/14/white-sox-all-stars-munetaka-murakami-miguel-vargas-tristan-peters-mlb-philadelphia-citizens-bank-park" target="_blank" ><u>alongside teammates</u></a> Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami and Tristan Peters. Adding salt to the wound were the pair of division rival shortstops who got in ahead of Montgomery: Royals superstar Bobby Witt Jr. (.280/.350/.451 with 13 homers entering play Monday) and Tigers rookie Kevin McGonigle (.282/.390/.425, nine homers).</p><p>Aside from his position-leading homer total, Montgomery arrived in Texas with the third-most RBI (57) and fourth-highest slugging percentage (.477) among shortstops.</p><p>“Of course I thought I should have been [an All-Star], but obviously it didn’t work out, and all I can do now is just respond,” Montgomery said. “I take that as like a little chip on my shoulder, I guess.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1b0000" himself, “but if that’s something out there that can give him an extra boost and put that chip on his shoulder, that’s great.”</p><p>“There are still lots of awesome awards you can go out and win by having a really good second half here,” Venable said.</p><p>Not helping Montgomery’s All-Star case were his 121 strikeouts before the break, second-most among shortstops and in the top six overall, symptomatic of his streaky nature at the plate.</p><p>“I've come to realize that I’m not sure how to characterize where Colson's at,” Venable said. “There are some at-bats where he looks maybe out of sync, and then in the same game, he’s hitting the game-winning homer.”</p><p>Montgomery acknowledged a few days off provided “a very good refresher mentally,” not just for him, but for a clubhouse that’s shouldering plenty of chips while stunning a baseball world that had it inked for another season of cellar-dwelling back in March.</p><p>“It just goes back to everyone still doubting a little,” Montgomery said. “We’re a good team, we’ve had success, and we’re very confident in ourselves. And I think that’s what’s most dangerous about a team, especially a young team. . . . I think we all have a chip on our shoulder, just because we want to keep proving everyone wrong, and prove ourselves right from spring training. This is what we expected.”</p><p></p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Jameson Taillon returns from injured list, but so does tendency to allow long ball
entries.summary: <p>When right-hander Jameson Taillon went on the injured list June 8 with a strained left hamstring, he was leading the major leagues in home runs allowed with 20.</p><p>Thanks to being away for six weeks, Taillon isn’t leading the majors anymore. But considering the first inning of his first start back Monday against the Tigers, he could be again soon.</p><p>Taillon allowed a three-run homer to Riley Greene and a solo shot to Dillon Dingler — among several hard-hit balls — to put the Cubs in an early hole.</p><p>The Athletics’ Jeffrey Springs entered the day having allowed a major-league-high 26 homers. At this rate, he could be surpassed soon.</p><p>Before the game, Cubs manager Craig Counsell said that Taillon’s execution had to be better. Clearly, that wasn’t the case in the first.</p><p>“When we talk about execution for a guy like Taillon, it’s, I can put a ball on the outside edge, or I can throw a ball [outside the zone], based on the aggressiveness of the hitter,” Counsell said. “And that matters for a guy like Taillon. That’s what these guys have the ability to do.</p><p>“And there’s a difference in that for the hitter. That’s what Jamo needs to do. The changeup has to be competitive; no free pitches. The hitter has to be responsible for all four balls or all three strikes. The locked-in mechanics allow you to do that.”</p><p>After the second homer, Taillon settled in, retiring 11 of the next 12 batters, five on strikeouts. But his tendency to give up the long ball in bunches remains an issue.</p><h3>Maton goes back on IL</h3><p>In addition to activating Taillon from the 15-day injured list, the Cubs added right-handed Aaron Civale to the 26-man roster, designated left-hander Drew Pomeranz for assignment and put righty Phil Maton on the injured list with tendinitis in his right knee.</p><p>Maton pitched one inning Sunday against the Twins, allowing one run, two hits and a walk, raising his ERA to 6.18. After signing a two-year, $14.5 million contract to be a key late-inning reliever, Maton is on the IL for the third time this season with the injury.</p><p>“We were all optimistic [about] some rest with the All-Star break, and he thought, we thought we were in a pretty good place,” Counsell said. “Symptoms again [Sunday]. Did an MRI, and the news is not great. We’re going to get some more opinions and see what that means. We’re looking at a little bit more extended absence.”</p><p>Pomeranz, 37, made six relief appearances, allowing five earned runs in 5 ⅔ innings.</p><p>“When Hoby [Milner] had the appendicitis, we had some runway for [Pomeranz],” Counsell said. “In the end, with a pretty clear [idea] that Hoby is going to be back and where we’re at and with our schedule of a lot of games the next 2 ½ weeks, it didn’t feel like Drew was going to be an answer long-term. And I thought the priority of the innings was pretty important right now.”</p><h3>Counsell: Palencia’s best to come</h3><p>Though right-hander Daniel Palencia is still several weeks from returning from a strained flexor, Counsell said he was confident that the closer would have time to recapture his old form.</p><p>“Daniel’s got a lot of runway to come back,” Counsell said. “I fully expect Daniel to be back pitching for us this year. I think he’s going to miss a length of time where we’re going to have to get him acclimated again. But I think he has plenty of time to get to the best version of himself this year. And I expect him to.</p><p>“He missed some time at the end of the season last year, and I thought we got a great version of Daniel.”</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-c90005" name="list-c90005"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, pageNumber=1, titleUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs, inverseColors=false, footerBgColor=#000000, title=Latest on the Cubs, bodyFont=font-3, showListNumbers=false, imagePositionHorizontal=null, rteBodyFont=font-3, headerBottomBorderColor=#111010, subTitle=null, stickyHeader=true, listTitleColor=#000000, tableCellBorderColor=#ccd1d5, relatedListFont=font-1, hideAuthors=true, tertiaryTextColor=#6c6c6c, buttonHoverTextColor=#ffffff, tableFont=font-1, carouselAutoPlay=false, promoTitleFont=font-2, ctaButtonText=[], primaryTextColor=#2a2a2a, buttonTextColor=#ffffff, linkTextColor=#1a1a1a, hideTitles=false, footerLinkColor=#ffffff, count=14106, pullQuoteIcon=[{image=null, narrowImage=null, _template=/image/Image.hbs, alt=null}], items=[{type=Image, description=[{items=[“The first two days just felt a little off,” Bregman said Sunday. “What we were working on right before the break felt better today. entries.title: Cubs' Alex Bregman feeling more comfortable at plate, and it's showing
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> third baseman Alex Bregman finally might have unlocked something in his swing.</p><p>Just as when teammate Dansby Swanson broke through ‘‘the dam’’ last month that had been keeping his hitting at bay, Bregman appears to have found ‘‘the feels’’ at the plate.</p><p>After hitting two home runs in June, Bregman was homerless this month until he went deep July 11-12 in Cincinnati. The second of those homers was accompanied by a single and a double, and Bregman drove in four runs.</p><p>Unfortunately for him, the All-Star break cost him those ‘‘feels,’’ and he went 0-for-7 in the first two games back, Friday and Saturday against the Twins. For reasons that defy explanation, the ‘‘feels’’ returned Sunday, when he hit a two-run homer in the first inning, giving him three homers in five games.</p><p>‘‘The first two days just felt a little off,’’ he said after the Cubs’ 10-1 victory. ‘‘What we were working on right before the break felt better today. We kind of figured out what was going wrong. So [I] felt good. The swing felt just like it did in Cincinnati, which was nice.</p><p>‘‘Feels better. Feels much simpler.’’</p><p>Feels. What does that mean?</p><p>‘‘Players are just trying to find feels that work for them,’’ manager Craig Counsell said. ‘‘That’s what Alex is referring to. The beauty of hitting and the madness of hitting is that it’s a constant life search for it, and it feels like, once I find it, why does it ever go away?</p><p>‘‘That’s why hitting’s hard. And that’s why you work and you practice and keep trying to find it. The feel is here today, and you might have to find a new one tomorrow.’’</p><p>Sometimes those feels are all a hitter needs to get back in the groove. If not for quadriceps injuries in 2021 with the Astros and last season with the Red Sox, Bregman probably would have entered this season coming off five in a row with 20 homers. He didn’t forget how to hit dingers, but that feeling of hitting them became elusive. His homer Sunday finally put him in double digits this season.</p><p>The Cubs stuck with Bregman, 32, during his drought because that’s what you do when you give someone a five-year, $175 million contract. And hitting was all he had to worry about Monday in the opener of a three-game series against the Tigers at Wrigley Field. Bregman was the designated hitter for only the sixth time this season.</p><p>Cubs president Jed Hoyer told the Sun-Times the team wanted to get Bregman off his feet while keeping his hot bat in the lineup. In his place at third, the Cubs gave another start to rookie Pedro Ramirez, who has his own hot bat. While going 2-for-4 as the DH on Sunday, Ramirez scalded three pitches at exit velocities faster than 100 mph.</p><p>In true baseball fashion, his biggest hit was his softest: a 75.5 mph ground-rule double.</p><p>‘‘He finished the first half not playing a lot, so he’s getting a little opportunity,’’ Counsell said. ‘‘He’s found some holes and had some good at-bats.’’</p><p>Bregman is having good at-bats, too, as Counsell also noted Sunday.</p><p>‘‘The swing in the first was really good,’’ he said of Bregman’s homer. ‘‘A couple of other hard-hit balls, for sure. Hard-hit balls [Saturday]. He’s putting some good swings on the baseball and driving the baseball, as well.’’</p><p>Indeed, Bregman smashed three pitches Sunday at exit velocities faster than 97 mph, two of them leading to outs and the other leaving the yard.</p><p>Bregman is capable of driving the Cubs’ offense, as long as those ‘‘feels’’ stick around.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 entries.title: Four beluga whales on way to Shedd from closed Canadian park: report
entries.summary: <p>Four beluga whales from a shuttered aquatic park in Niagara Falls, Canada, were on their way to Shedd Aquarium Monday as part of an “unprecedented rescue effort,” according to Canadian media.</p><p>Two more whales were headed to SeaWorld in San Antonio Monday, <a class="Link" href="https://www.winnipegfreepress.com/canada/2026/07/20/cp-newsalert-six-whales-being-moved-out-of-marineland-headed-to-u-s" target="_blank" >according to The Canadian Press</a>.</p><p>It’s the first phase of a plan to move up to 30 belugas over the next few weeks from Marineland to several American aquariums as well as to Oceanografic Valencia in Spain. Earlier this month, Shedd announced it could receive as many as 10 belugas from Marineland.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-500000" name="image-500000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b239233/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3564x2000+0+188/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb4%2F8e%2Ff031ac824be5a807800df78fa12b%2Fbeluga-marineland-truck-transport.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5946204/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3564x2000+0+188/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb4%2F8e%2Ff031ac824be5a807800df78fa12b%2Fbeluga-marineland-truck-transport.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/80a0fda/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3564x2000+0+188/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb4%2F8e%2Ff031ac824be5a807800df78fa12b%2Fbeluga-marineland-truck-transport.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="One of the trucks, holding a blue water tank, in which beluga whales were to be transported from the now-closed Marineland in Niagara Falls, Canada. entries.title: Dear Abby: Relatives weigh wedding gift for undeserving nephew
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Our nephew "Conrad" is engaged to be married soon. For several reasons, we are unable to attend the wedding. Under normal circumstances, I wouldn't hesitate to send a generous gift as I have for our other nieces and nephews. However, Conrad is not normal. He doesn't speak to me, my husband or our children, two of whom are his age. We have never done anything to offend him, as far as I know, and it's not just our family. He also ignores other specific family members.</p><p>Conrad's mother describes him as "the kindest" and "most loving" person. However, we have never seen that side of him. We have witnessed only narcissism and rudeness. He speaks only to those he thinks elevate his status or make him look good in some way. If, according to Conrad, we do not exist, are we still obligated to send a wedding gift? — <i>INVISIBLE IN THE SOUTHERN PLAINS</i></p><p><b>DEAR INVISIBLE:</b> Are you certain you will receive a wedding invitation from this nephew? Technically, if you don't attend, you're not required to give him anything. However, in light of the fact that you have been generous to your other nieces and nephews, it might be more diplomatic to send a less expensive token gift to mollify his parents.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have been married for 10 years. For the first three years, I tried to get closer to my in-laws but was told I wasn't welcome. I knew they didn't like me, but I tried my hardest to win them over because family is important to me. In the end, I was asked to leave their house. My husband was on my side, but I realized I couldn't separate him from his family. So, for seven years he's had the support of his family and mine.</p><p>One of his siblings is now sick, and it's looking grim. I do not feel my presence is required at the funeral as no one in his family likes me. Am I wrong? Anytime I run into his family, they are confrontational. — <i>STAYING AWAY IN ILLINOIS</i></p><p><b>DEAR STAYING AWAY:</b> Ask your husband if he would like your emotional support at his sibling's funeral. Bear in mind that funerals do not bring out the best in some people, and your in-laws will be no exception. Then do as your husband requests but have a quick getaway plan in place in case you need to leave.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Two of our children are planning a European vacation with their families. My wife is upset because they didn't invite her and stated bluntly that she's not welcome to join them. How can we convince her not to take their decision personally? — <i>MAYBE NEXT TIME IN MASSACHUSETTS</i></p><p><b>DEAR MAYBE:</b> Surely your wife is mature enough to understand that when a young family takes a trip, she should not expect to be automatically included? They are entitled to some time to make memories together. If she insists on taking it personally, there is nothing you can do to convince her, so let her sulk it out.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>For everything you need to know about wedding planning, order "How to Have a Lovely Wedding." Send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds), to: Dear Abby, Wedding Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: Berwyn Eagles Club has a new owner. What does that mean for Chicago wrestling?
entries.summary: <p>Months after the storied wrestling venue <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/04/24/berwyn-eagles-club-wrestling-fight-venue-aaw-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>stopped hosting matches</u></a>, the Berwyn Eagles Club has a new owner.</p><p>The property at 6309 W. 26th St. in Berwyn has been sold to the neighboring Berwyn Auto Spa, confirmed owner José Tejada. The car wash <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DaOnh_buxNA/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><u>posted a video</u></a> on its Instagram page that showed the former Eagles Club with a new name: Destino.</p><p>According to the post, the building will be converted into an event space. The new owner and Auto Spa staff did not respond to multiple requests for additional comment about the future of the former Eagles Club, or what types of events they plan to host in the space.</p><p>The auto spa business, at 6307 W. 26th St., offers hand-washing and detailing. It also operates a Harold’s Chicken and a full bar offering beer and cocktails for customers to enjoy while their vehicles are being serviced.</p><p>But a <a class="Link" href="https://berwynauto-spa.com/" target="_blank" ><u>website</u></a> for the auto spa space does not list any upcoming events. entries.title: CPD officer's gun discharges while arresting suspect with alleged stolen vehicle in North Lawndale
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago police officer's weapon discharged during an attempt to arrest a suspect accused of being in possession of a stolen vehicle early Tuesday in North Lawndale on the West Side. </p><p>Around 3:40 a.m., 10th District officers in the 1600 block of South Drake Avenue and were trying to arrest a male for possessing a stolen vehicle when he tried to disarm an office, police said. </p><p>One officer's weapon discharged during the struggle, authorities said. No one was struck by gunfire. </p><p>The officer suffered minor injuries and was taken to an area hospital in fair condition, officials said. </p><p>The suspect was arrested and taken to Mount Sinai Hospital for minor injuries, according to police. </p><p>The officers involved in the shooting will be placed on routine administrative duties for at least 30 days. </p><p>The Civilian Office of Police Accountability was investigating the shooting. </p>

James</a></h5><p><b>Deadly toll</b>: Six people in Cook County have died from heat-related causes in July so far, marking the deadliest stretch of extreme hot-weather deaths since at least 2015. Four of those who died were younger than 60.</p><p><b>Lives lost</b>: Victor Ferguson, 48, died July 2 from heat stroke with ethanol intoxication as a secondary cause, according to new records from the Cook County medical examiner's office. Others whose deaths have been attributed to the heat, according to the medical examiner's office, are Stephanie Rodriguez, 45; David Gonzalez, 44; Barbara Whigham, 71; Mike Rodriguez, 57; and Daniel Machnikowski, 69. One death happened in Evanston. The others who died were residents of Chicago's South and West sides.</p><p><b>Key factors</b>: Communities in the South and West sides are most vulnerable to extreme heat, according to one expert, who says some of that vulnerability is tied to socioeconomic factors, like not being able to afford an elevated electricity bill to cool a home or not having an adequate air conditioning unit. Neighborhoods with fewer trees also provide less shade during extreme heat.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wujkyky-l-u/" target="_blank" ><b>READ >Sarah Karp</a></h5><h5></h5><p><b>Specialized needs</b>: A growing group of students in Chicago Public Schools has autism and needs special education — a new reality for the school district that has major academic and financial implications. </p><p><b>Rise in needs</b>: As of this spring, almost 83,000 students qualified for an individualized education program, which legally requires school districts to provide students with specialized education services or to remove barriers to their learning. That's 26% of CPS students, up from 20% in 2019. It's a national trend that's more pronounced in Chicago. </p><p><b>Separate rooms, more staff</b>: The number of students with autism has doubled since 2019, according to CPS data. Many of them require intensive classroom support and therapy, and a growing number spend the majority of their day in separate classes. When CPS recently announced <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wujkyky-l-jy/" target="_blank" >Stefano Esposito</a></h5><p><b>Whales on the way</b>: Four beluga whales from a shuttered aquatic park in Niagara Falls, Canada, were on their way to Shedd Aquarium on Monday as part of an "unprecedented rescue effort," according to Canadian media. It's the first phase of a plan to move up to 30 belugas over the next few weeks from Marineland to several U.S. aquariums and to Oceanografic Valencia in Spain. Shedd announced it could receive as many as 10 belugas.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: The future of the belugas has been in doubt since Marineland closed to the public in 2024. Marineland has previously threatened to euthanize the sea mammals, citing a lack of funding to care for them. Twenty whales have died at Marineland since 2019, AP reported.</p><p><b>Controversial move</b>: Some animal rights advocates argue that the whales are being exported potentially in violation of a 2019 Canadian law that bans the breeding of marine mammals in captivity.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wujkyky-l-jj/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>ON WBEZ 91.5 FM 📻 </h4><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wujkyky-l-jd/" target="_blank" ><b>In the Loop with Sasha-Ann Simons, 9 a.m.</b></a></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="line-height: inherit; margin-top: 0px; margin-bottom: 20px; margin-left: 24px; padding: 0px; list-style-type: disc;" id="rte-833a8593-8504-11f1-821f-41c27a23c2f6"><li><b>Addressing heat</b>: How do we keep residents in the hottest neighborhoods cool during heat waves? Nedra Sims-Fears of the Greater Chatham Initiative, Max Berkelhammer of University of Illinois at Chicago and Lindy Wordlaw of the Chicago Department of Environment explain.<br></li><li><b>WNBA All-Star Weekend</b>: Twenty-two of the league's best players take over the Bulls' court this weekend. to paint Evanston wall</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wujkyky-l-tk/" target="_blank" >Genevieve Bookwalter</a></h5><p>Four friends who grew up graffitiing Evanston walls returned to their hometown this month to add more color and to celebrate the addition of a new "permission wall" for the next generation of writers.</p><p>Garrett Munski, Ole Flores, Alex Mendoza and Jordan Nickel grew up tagging walls, viaducts, underpasses and more as kids in Evanston in the 1990s and early 2000s. Nickel built his adult career around creating art, working under the artist name POSE. Munski went on to work as a mechanic while Flores is a CPA. Mendoza owns his own sign company.</p><p>The four reunited this time to legally paint a wall on Green Bay Road at Simpson Street. Johnny Cash and Buena Vista Social Club blasted while the four created their individual panels with color and spray cans.</p><p>The wall is the precursor to a permissible graffiti wall scheduled to open later this summer on the other side of the same wall, facing an overgrown empty lot.</p><p>The four men reminisced about their high school days while they completed the strokes and shading with their cans.</p><p>Flores said the new mural was the first piece he had painted in 20 years. "Time passes. The passion doesn’t," he said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wujkyky-l-tu/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><i>What tips do you have for fighting off mosquitoes?</i> </p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply here with your answer</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). We may run your answer in a future newsletter or story.</i></p><p>On Monday, we asked you: <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wujkyky-l-il/" target="_blank" >What’s the best way to make a new friend as an adult?</a></p><p>Here’s some of what you said…</p><p>"I had great luck finding friends as an adult when I reached out to my child's friend's family members. We were able to do things together, with and without our children. Also, through volunteering locally." — <i>Christine Bock</i></p><p>"Find a club, church, activity or team that interests you. You'll find others [who] share your interest so you automatically have something to talk about. Teodo</i></p><p>"Salsa classes!" — <i>Ronnie Saso</i></p><p>"Join an adult sports league or do group travel." — <i>Noah Buckwalter</i></p><p>"Go to your local watering hole the same day and time for a few weeks; you will start to recognize people and before you know it, you will have new friends." — <i>Tom Carter</i></p><p>For some more ideas, listen to callers' suggestions on Monday's <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wujkyky-l-ir/" target="_blank" >Say More with Mary Dixon & Patrick Smith</a>.</p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Eydie Cubarrubia</p><hr><p><i>The Chicago Sun-Times is a nonprofit supported by readers like you. entries.title: Chicago's air quality has improved, but experts caution ongoing wildfires, wind can change conditions
entries.summary: <p>The air quality in Chicago has improved after days of unhealthy conditions due to smoke from Canadian wildfires — but the area isn’t entirely out of the woods. </p><p>As <a class="Link" href="https://cwfis.cfs.nrcan.gc.ca/en/" target="_blank" >nearly 900 wildfires</a> continue to burn throughout Canada, experts say the fires and weather patterns like wind direction may change the local air quality going forward. </p><p>"Based on the wildfire episodes our city has experienced in the summers of 2023, 2025, and this year, residents should expect periods of changing air quality, depending on Canadian and U.S. West Coast wildfire activity and weather patterns," said Serap Erdal, associate professor at the University of Illinois Environmental and Occupational Health Sciences School of Public Health.</p><p></p><p>Late last week, Chicago’s Air Quality Index ranged from very unhealthy to hazardous, the two most severe levels on the Air Quality Index. The conditions were caused by a cold front that carried wildfire smoke to the ground level in Illinois, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. </p><p>"Smoke is heavily influenced by the weather," a spokesperson with the EPA said. "Just as weather can change hour to hour, so can the AQI."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/16/wildfire-smoke-prompts-air-quality-alert-for-most-of-chicago-area-to" target="_blank" >‘Hazardous’ Canadian wildfire smoke prompts air quality warning for Chicago. Here’s what you should know.</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Generally, an AQI value below 100 is considered acceptable for air quality, while anything over 100 first becomes unhealthy for sensitive groups before becoming unhealthy for everyone as the values increase. </p><p>For any value over 301, the air is considered hazardous and all sensitive groups are urged to stay indoors while everyone else is encouraged to avoid lengthy amounts of time outdoors. </p><p>As of Tuesday morning, Chicago's Air Quality Index was around 50, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.airnow.gov/?city=Chicago&state=IL&country=USA" target="_blank" >EPA’s AirNow website</a>. </p><p>"As air quality improves in the Chicago area, the health risk from wildfire smoke will diminish when AQI levels drop to 100 or lower," Erdal noted. </p><p>The rapidly changing air quality conditions is something Chicago area residents will need to get used to every summer. More intense forest fires in Canada are happening earlier as climate change is producing warmer spring temperatures and dryness up north. <a class="Link" href="https://yaleclimateconnections.org/2026/07/dangerous-and-historic-wildfire-smoke-pollution-event-engulfs-the-u-s-and-canada/" target="_blank" >Researchers sugges</a>t that some of those fires will continue to burn for months, impacting air quality across much of North America.</p><p>Fires create fine particulate matter, or PM 2.5, that can lodge deep into your lungs and travel through your blood once inhaled. These microscopic particles are particularly dangerous for people with asthma and other medical conditions or weak immune systems. They can lead to heart attacks and strokes after exposure for long periods.</p><p>To avoid health issues due to wildfire smoke, experts stressed the importance of checking the AQI before going outside, staying indoors until the AQI drops to under 100, wearing an N95 or KN95 mask if they need to be outside and setting their air conditioners to "recirculate" mode to ensure outdoor air is not pulled indoors. </p><p>“I think everyone should close their doors and windows to try to prevent the smoke from getting into their homes as much as possible,” said Dr. Jack Zhao, a pulmonary critical care doctor at Rush Copley Medical Center. “I equate being outside with a forest fire to smoking. I think over time it will cause long-term side effects.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Brett Chase, Haley</i> <i>Blomquist</i></p>

entries.title: Photos: Rick Ross brings his Port of Miami 20th Anniversary Tour to Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Rick Ross, the self-proclaimed B.O.A.T. (biggest of all time), sailed into Chicago last week as part of his Port of Miami 20th Anniversary Black-Tie Experience tour, featuring Chicago rapper Twista as special guest.</p><p>The Friday performance at Chicago Theatre coincided with the release of not just the hip-hop legend’s 2006 debut, “Port of Miami,” but also his 12th album, “Set In Stone.” </p><p>Appearing with the Renaissance entries.title: White Sox place catcher Kyle Teel on 10-day injured list with ankle sprain, recall Edgar Quero
entries.summary: <p>ARLINGTON, Texas — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> entered the year with perhaps the most promising duo of young catchers in baseball.</p><p>But in a season full of positive surprises, the Sox are dealing with another tough one as Kyle Teel’s latest injury has them hoping that a struggling Edgar Quero can regain his form at the plate.</p><p>The Sox placed Teel on the 10-day injured list Tuesday, a day after he suffered an ankle injury while trying to tag out a runner at the plate during their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/20/kyle-teel-injury-white-sox-rangers" target="_blank" ><u>series opening win in Texas</u></a>. It looked like it could’ve been a lot worse when manager Will Venable and head athletic trainer James Kruk had to help Teel off the field.</p><p>It’s the third injury Teel has weathered in his sophomore season. The 24-year-old pulled a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/11/white-sox-catcher-kyle-teel-suffers-grade-2-right-hamstring-strain-in-team-italys-world-baseball-classic-win" target="_blank" ><u>hamstring</u></a> while running out a double for Team Italy in the World Baseball Classic, then tweaked a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/17/new-knee-issue-adds-to-intrigue-surrounding-white-sox-catcher-kyle-teel" target="_blank" ><u>knee ligament</u></a> when he initially was nearing a return in mid-May.</p><p>Teel’s latest setback came less than a month after making it back to the Sox on June 22. He’d hit .190/.271/.317 with two homers, two doubles and 14 RBI in 19 games.</p><p>The team recalled Quero, who never found a rhythm at the plate while handling the bulk of catching duties in Teel’s initial absence. After showing a knack for contact his rookie season, Quero labored to a paltry .187/.253/.233 line in 55 games to start this season.</p><p>He did produce one of the season’s top highlights with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/17/edgar-quero-white-sox-rally-past-cubs-to-take-crosstown-series" >a walk-off homer against the Cubs</a> at Rate Field to secure a crosstown series win.</p><p>But Quero only hit one other homer and a double, and the 23-year-old didn’t fare much better after getting shipped to Triple-A following Teel’s comeback. In 15 games with Charlotte, Quero hit .230/.299/.295 with a homer, a double and six RBI.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-4a0005" name="list-4a0005"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, items=[{type=Image, anchorId=promo-350000, description=[{items=[The Sox went on to win 10-3, but they face big questions behind the plate with the trade deadline looming.]}], _styledTemplate=null, imageAlignment=null, categoryUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox, isFeatured=false, publishDate=July 20, 2026 10:49 PM, timestamp=1784605740000, category=[{items=[White Sox]}], target=null, primaryMediaType=null, title=Kyle Teel likely headed back to IL after ugly ankle injury during White Sox win at Texas, authors=[{ampLink=null, _styledTemplate=null, _template=/author/byline/AuthorByline.hbs, media=[{alt=Mitchell Armentrout, ampLink=null, _styledTemplate=null, _template=/image/Image.hbs, image={src=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/fc/ce/f20d6ee54780a793233d9b8dc7ef/armentrout-01.jpg, width=5053, height=3370}, narrowImage={src=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/fc/ce/f20d6ee54780a793233d9b8dc7ef/armentrout-01.jpg, width=5053, height=3370}}], bio=[{items=[Mitchell Armentrout is a staff reporter covering government and politics from Chicago to Springfield, focusing on the expansion of gambling across Illinois as well as the Chicago Bears’ quest for a new stadium. entries.title: Two independent candidates won't appear on November ballot for Rep. Garcia's seat, state board rules
entries.summary: <p>Two independent candidates vying for U.S. Rep. Jesus "Chuy" Garcia's Congressional seat will not appear on the November ballot after the Illinois State Board of Elections on Tuesday ruled that both did not submit the minimum number of valid petition signatures — 10,816 required to run as an independent candidate.</p><p>Both Mayra Macías and Ald. Byron Sigcho-Lopez (25th) will not appear on the ballot, leaving Lyons Mayor Chris Getty as the only independent to make it to the ballot. There were no challenges filed against Getty's petitions. Patty Garcia, Rep. Garcia's chief of staff, is running for his seat after the congressman <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2025/11/03/jesus-chuy-garcia-reelection-dropping-out-chief-of-staff-running" target="_blank" >abruptly dropped out of the race</a> and raised eyebrows by quickly helping her get enough signatures to make a tight deadline. </p><p>The board ruled unanimously that both candidates did not get the required number of signatures. </p><p>State Board of Elections general counsel Marni M. Malowitz said Mayra Macías submitted 9,758 valid signatures, which is 1,058 fewer than was required. In one instance, a petitioner provided a wrong home address, so 101 of the signatures she collected were tossed. In another, a petition circulator was also getting signatures from other Democratic candidates, which is not allowed for independent candidates. In other cases, signatures were not valid.</p><p>"More than 30,000 voters signed petitions for me and Ald. Sigcho-Lopez [collectively]. Those signatures represent 30,000 conversations with people... " Macías said. "Despite the extraordinary threshold, our campaign knocked on over 50,000 doors and submitted over 17,000 signatures, more than enough to demonstrate broad community support and way more signatures than Patty Garcia submitted, or Congressman Garcia has ever submitted."</p><p>Macías, who was at the hearing, criticized the process, saying she was given just three days to prove many signatures were legitimate. She also said "the spirit of the law is being completely broken in this race."</p><p>"The rules were put in place to safeguard democracy, and yet these very rules are currently doing the opposite," Macías said. </p><p>Malowitz said Sigcho-Lopez submitted 9,594 valid signatures, which is 1,222 fewer than required. </p><p>Malowitz noted that the constitutional challenges that Sigcho-Lopez presented weren't under the board's jurisdiction and said "they should be raised by the courts." Among those objections were signers of an independent candidate's position don't have to be registered voters or to write their address next to their names on a petition sheet. Malowitz said she agreed with objectors that election code does require signers be registered to vote at an address listed.</p><p>In the face of challenges to their candidacies, Sigcho-Lopez and Macias are teaming up to call for changes to the state’s process for independent candidates, which they say is set up to help established Democrats stay in power. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-790000" name="image-790000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d3a3c02/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F28%2Faf%2F00bf12d24d0d83f71eb93ac38e18%2F186a0803.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/21edb4e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F28%2Faf%2F00bf12d24d0d83f71eb93ac38e18%2F186a0803.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a423007/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F28%2Faf%2F00bf12d24d0d83f71eb93ac38e18%2F186a0803.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. entries.title: Policía de Chicago fue uno de dos heridos durante situación de atrincheramiento en Albany Park
entries.summary: <p>Un sospechoso fue arrestado el lunes después de que supuestamente le disparara a un oficial de la Policía de Chicago y a otra persona durante una situación de atrincheramiento en Albany Park, en el lado noroeste de la ciudad.</p><p>La policía respondió a eso de las 11 a.m. a una llamada sobre una mujer herida de bala en la cuadra 4600 al norte de Springfield Avenue, dijo el superintendente interino de la Policía de Chicago, Fred Waller, a los reporteros el lunes por la tarde. Un informe interno de la policía indicó que le habían disparado en la cara.</p><p>Los oficiales encontraron que el sospechoso masculino se había atrincherado dentro de una casa con una adolescente y una mujer mayor que podría haber sido su novia, añadió Waller. La alerta de la policía describió a la niña como de 13 años.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ca0000" name="module-ca0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Cuando los oficiales de Armas y Tácticas Especiales (SWAT) intentaron ingresar a la casa, el sospechoso disparó a través de una puerta y alcanzó a uno de los oficiales en la parte baja del abdomen, según Waller.</p><p>Ambas víctimas de los disparos fueron trasladadas rápidamente al Centro Médico Masonic Advocate Illinois, donde Waller dijo que la mujer estaba en estado grave y que el oficial fue sometido a una cirugía de inmediato. Afuera del hospital, Waller comentó que la condición del oficial se había estabilizado y que estaba siendo visitado por su familia.</p><p>El oficial herido ha trabajado para el Departamento de Policía de Chicago (CPD) durante aproximadamente 20 años y fue miembro de la unidad SWAT durante más de una década, dijo Waller.</p><p>Waller informó que las dos mujeres retenidas por el sospechoso habían sido "agredidas". Dijo que fueron llevadas al Hospital Stroger con lesiones que no se consideraban potencialmente mortales.</p><p>El sospechoso fue detenido y se le estaba procesando, indicó Waller. Los investigadores estaban determinando si tenía antecedentes de violencia doméstica.</p><p>Al hablar junto a Waller, el alcalde Brandon Johnson expresó que la Ciudad estaba "increíblemente agradecida por el trabajo rápido y activo de nuestro Departamento de Policía".</p><p>"Es lamentable que la violencia doméstica exista de la manera en que lo hace en esta ciudad", añadió Johnson. "Estamos agradecidos de que [los oficiales] hayan podido desescalar la situación para prevenir daños mayores".</p><h3>‘Tenemos un oficial de SWAT herido’</h3><p>Los oficiales respondieron inicialmente alrededor de las 10:55 a.m. a una llamada al 911 de una mujer herida de bala en la cara, según el tráfico de radio de la policía. Cerca de 10 minutos después, se autorizó una respuesta de SWAT para atender a un sospechoso atrincherado dentro de la casa.</p><p>Durante el enfrentamiento, una mujer llamó al 911 desde el interior de la casa y se le oía suplicando al sospechoso.</p><p>"Por favor, no dispares por la puerta", dijo la llamada.</p><p>"Está tratando de convencerlo de que baje el arma. Tengan cuidado, muchachos", dijo un despachador a los oficiales que respondían.</p><p>Alrededor de las 11:45 a.m., una llamada de "oficial en peligro" atravesó las ondas de comunicación.</p><p>"Tenemos un oficial de SWAT herido, muchachos, en la parte trasera. Tenemos un oficial de SWAT herido", dijo el despachador.</p><p>Poco después de que el oficial fuera herido, la mujer le estaba suplicando al hombre que apagara el gas, según el radio de la policía.</p><p>"Está llorando y diciéndole que apague el gas. Él ha encendido el gas", dijo un despachador. "La mujer sigue suplicándole que apague el gas, le ruega que baje el arma y se acueste para que nadie más resulte herido".</p><p>Varios minutos después, la mujer agradeció al hombre después de que, al parecer, apagó el gas, según el radio.</p><p>"Le estaba agradeciendo por apagar el gas, supongo que apagó el gas", dijo el despachador.</p><h3>Los vecinos se sienten inseguros</h3><p>Algunos vecinos que se acercaron a la escena expresaron su preocupación por el crimen en el vecindario del lado noroeste.</p><p>Alvin Woodley dijo que ha vivido en Albany Park durante siete años y que no siempre se siente seguro, especialmente por la noche.</p><p>Woodley, de 56 años, recordó que un niño fue herido de bala en el pecho en un parque cercano el año pasado mientras los niños jugaban al baloncesto. Dijo que los vecinos pueden ser reacios a llamar a la policía y a reportar lo que ven.</p><p>"Creo que mucha gente simplemente no quiere involucrarse", comentó Woodley. “La estación de policía está justo a la vuelta de la esquina, así que no debería haber tanto crimen".</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a entries.title: WNBA announces three-point contest field for All-Star weekend
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/wnba" >WNBA’s</a> three-point contest is returning to Wintrust Arena.</p><p>All-Stars Marina Mabrey of the Tempo and Rhyne Howard of the Dream headline the six-player field announced Tuesday. They will be joined by No. 1 overall pick Azzi Fudd of the Wings, Bridget Carleton of the Fire, Natisha Hiedeman of the Storm and Janelle Salaün of the Valkyries.</p><p>The contest will begin at 7 p.m. Friday and air on ESPN as part of the opening night of WNBA All-Star festivities. The league’s new Shooting Stars competition will also take place that night at Wintrust Arena, though participants have not yet been announced.</p><p>The field features six of the league’s 10 best three-point shooters this season. Mabrey leads the WNBA with 82 made three-pointers, followed by Howard with 79. Salaün ranks fifth with 67, Carleton sixth with 65 and Hiedeman seventh with 57. Fudd is tied for 10th with 50.</p><p>Still, the list of players who will not participate is notable.</p><p>Sabrina Ionescu, who won the contest last season and also captured the title in 2023, will not defend her crown. Caitlin Clark, the the league’s most recognizable three-point shooter, also is not participating. Other prominent omissions include Kelsey Mitchell, Kayla McBride and Kelsey Plum.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> have not had a player in the contest since Allie Quigley won it in Chicago in 2022. It was Quigley’s record fourth title, the most by any player in WNBA or NBA history.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Seis muertes relacionadas con el calor hacen de julio el mes más mortal en más de una década
entries.summary: <p>Seis personas en el Condado de Cook han muerto por causas relacionadas con el calor en lo que va de julio, marcando el período más mortal de muertes por calor extremo desde al menos 2015.</p><p>Victor Ferguson, de 48 años, es la última persona identificada que murió durante la ola de calor este mes. Ferguson falleció el 2 de julio por un golpe de calor, con intoxicación por etanol como causa secundaria, según nuevos registros de la Oficina del Médico Forense del Condado de Cook.</p><p>Cuatro de las seis personas fallecidas tenían menos de 60 años. En total, hasta ahora se han registrado seis muertes durante este mes en el Condado de Cook, con temperaturas altas que oscilaban entre 88 y 95 grados el día en que fallecieron o fueron hospitalizados, según un análisis de datos del Servicio Meteorológico Nacional (NWS) realizado por WBEZ y el Chicago Sun-Times. Durante la primera semana de julio, al acercarse el fin de semana del Cuatro de Julio, el Condado de Cook estaba bajo una advertencia de calor extremo.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fa0000" name="module-fa0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Además de Ferguson, las otras personas cuyas muertes han sido atribuidas al calor son Stephanie Rodríguez, de 45 años; David González, de 44; Barbara Whigham, de 71; Mike Rodríguez, de 57; y Daniel Machnikowski, de 69, según la Oficina del Médico Forense.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-cb0000" name="html-embed-module-cb0000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/29744387"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/29744387/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Desde la ola de calor de Chicago en 1995, que mató a más de 700 personas, la ciudad ha sufrido al menos otras dos olas de calor mortales: <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2016/8/30/18354264/a-look-back-at-chicago-s-deadly-1995-heat-wave" target="_blank" >en 1999, cuando murieron 10 personas, y en 2012, cuando fallecieron 22.</a></p><p>Marc Raifman, quien trabaja con la Coalición de Planificadores de Climas Extremos, dijo que los funcionarios de la Ciudad deberían trabajar con miembros de la comunidad para examinar las circunstancias que llevaron a las muertes de este mes.</p><p>“¿Por qué no estamos revisando estos casos, tratando de averiguar con cierto nivel de detalle, tal como lo hacen en el ámbito médico, qué salió mal que llevó a alguien a sufrir una lesión por calor o frío que, en algunos casos horribles, le costó la vida?”, cuestionó Raifman. “¿Y qué podemos hacer para prevenirlo la próxima vez y salvar a la próxima persona?”.</p><p>Ferguson, la fatalidad relacionada con el calor más reciente, vivía en el vecindario de East Garfield Park en el lado oeste. Su familia no pudo ser contactada de inmediato.</p><p>Los vecinos recordaron que Ferguson vivía con su familia en una casa de dos pisos de piedra caliza. Se podían ver unidades de aire acondicionado en el primer y en el segundo piso.</p><p>También dijeron que Ferguson a menudo se le veía caminando con sus dos perros.</p><p>Los vecinos de Rodríguez dijeron que compartía una casa con varios familiares. Rodríguez, añadieron, vivía en el ático, que no tenía buena circulación de aire. Una unidad de aire acondicionado se veía montada en una ventana del ático la mañana del lunes.</p><p>Los familiares y amigos de los otros fallecidos se negaron a hacer comentarios o no pudieron ser contactados, incluyendo un familiar de Rodríguez que vivía en la misma casa y que el lunes se negó a comentar.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>La dirección donde el Médico Forense del Condado de Cook dijo que vivía Mike Rodríguez cuando murió por complicaciones relacionadas con el calor en McKinley Park. En la ventana frontal del ático, donde los vecinos dijeron que él vivía, se ve un aire acondicionado de ventana.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Una muerte ocurrió en Evanston, y las otras cinco personas que murieron eran residentes de los lados sur y oeste de Chicago.</p><p>Las comunidades en los lados sur y oeste de Chicago son las más vulnerables al calor extremo, dijo Daniel Horton, profesor asociado en la Universidad Northwestern, quien ayudó a desarrollar un índice de vulnerabilidad al calor para la ciudad.</p><p>Parte de esa vulnerabilidad está relacionada con factores socioeconómicos, como no poder pagar una factura de electricidad elevada para enfriar una casa o no contar con una unidad de aire acondicionado adecuada, dijo Horton.</p><p>Los vecindarios con menos árboles también ofrecen menos sombra durante el calor extremo, lo que es una de las razones por las que los grupos comunitarios abogan por más sombra cerca de las paradas de autobús.</p><p>Pero un problema mayor a abordar es el aislamiento social, dijo Horton, refiriéndose a uno de los problemas más grandes que surgieron de la <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2015/7/11/18609460/chicago-1995-heat-wave-anniversary" target="_blank" >devastadora ola de calor de 1995</a>. Las personas eran más propensas a morir si no estaban conectadas con vecinos que podían estar al tanto de su bienestar o proporcionarles un ventilador u otros objetos para ayudarles a mantenerse frescas.</p><p>“Ese aspecto de la infraestructura social también es clave para aumentar la resiliencia de una comunidad”, destacó Horton.</p><p>Los grupos comunitarios también han presionado no sólo por un centro de enfriamiento de 24 horas, sino también por uno que mantenga sus puertas abiertas los fines de semana o días festivos, dijo Raifman. La Ciudad tiene estándares para activar una respuesta de emergencia por el clima, pero esos estándares pueden parecer inalcanzables, añadió.</p><p>La Ciudad a veces extiende el horario de cierre hasta las 8 p.m. en su centro de servicios comunitarios ubicado en 10 S. Kedzie Ave., según la oficina del alcalde.</p><p>La oficina del alcalde Brandon Johnson también dijo que los funcionarios estaban monitoreando de cerca las altas temperaturas, añadiendo que consideran que las estaciones de policía, bibliotecas, colegios comunitarios y las instalaciones del Distrito de Parques forman parte de los esfuerzos de enfriamiento en toda la ciudad. En un comunicado, la oficina del alcalde expresó que estaba “profundamente consternada por cualquier pérdida de vida relacionada con el clima en nuestra ciudad” y ofreció sus condolencias.</p><p>“Hay líderes e individuos en la ciudad que están trabajando arduamente en este momento para abordar estas situaciones”, dijo Raifman. “Pero creo que lo que les falta y lo que nos falta es algún tipo de planificación avanzada y comprensión de lo que se despliega y de dónde”.</p><p><i>Contribuyeron: Cam Rodríguez, Mohammad Samra y Alden Loury </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Save A Lot stores set to close Saturday after years of turmoil, recent CEO death threatens city-funded deal
entries.summary: <p>After opening seven Save A Lot discount grocery stores on Chicago’s South and West sides with a promise to address food deserts, embattled operator Yellow Banana is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/06/06/save-a-lot-yellow-banana-canfield-death-default-chicago-food-access-redevelopment-deal" target="_blank" >set to shutter all stores</a> this weekend, leaving some predominantly Black and brown neighborhoods without a grocery store.</p><p>Save A Lot says it’s cutting ties with Yellow Banana and will “end [its] arrangement,” company spokesperson Sarah Griffin said in a statement. Without Save A Lot corporate’s support, operator Yellow Banana will close all its stores, a few years after promising residents they would undo reputational damage to the Save A Lot brand.</p><p>“Financial headwinds” under Yellow Banana’s ownership are the cause of terminating the relationship, Griffin said. Save A Lot points to “dramatic cuts to SNAP benefits,” as significant challenges. </p><p>The company was unable to find a path forward to keep the stores open and notified Yellow Banana at the end of June that it would be terminating its operational agreement. </p><p>The end of the arrangement means Yellow Banana will have to find its own way out of the taxpayer-funded deal with the city or close six locations by Saturday if it does not find an alternative, according to Save A Lot.</p><p>Ohio-based operator Yellow Banana has a redevelopment agreement with the city of Chicago, for which it received over $13 million in taxpayer financing to renovate and reopen the stores. On top of the taxpayer funding, Save A Lot has requested an additional $3 million from the city recoup funds given to Yellow Banana, according to Ald. Marty Quinn (13th).</p><p>Quinn said he was told the stores were in danger of closing last week by Save A Lot. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Strazzabosco.</p><p>Save A Lot, which has a licensing agreement with Yellow Banana, went above and beyond the agreement terms to help out the operator financially and operationally.</p><p>Griffin has Since then, it has helped financially support Yellow Banana stores, despite not appearing in the redevelopment agreement between Yellow Banana and the city.</p><p>After years of delayed timelines, millions in lawsuits, fines and closures Yellow Banana was dealt its largest blow in April when CEO Joe Canfield died of a stroke, the Sun-Times reported last month. He was 54.</p><p>The death of the Ohio-based entrepreneur triggered a potential default in the city of Chicago’s redevelopment agreement. Yellow Banana was required to submit a succession plan, the Department of Planning and Development said at the time. No plan had been submitted as of last month.</p><p>Quinn said residents in his ward waited the longest for the West Lawn store at 4439 W. 63rd St. to open, after years of delays. The location opened in April 2025, the last of the stores to open.</p><p> “It’s very ... unfortunate, this development," he said on Tuesday. “I've been in contact with Commissioner [Ciere] Boatright who’s exploring all avenues of opportunity right now to keep the lights on.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a When they opened, residents were overjoyed at the opening of the stores. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>His residents have to head to the suburbs to get groceries without Save A Lot, he said.<br><b></b><br>Strazzabosco said the recent death of Canfield contributed as well to the ending of the agreement.</p><p>Canfield’s death was largely kept quiet, and no obituary or social media posts could be found from loved ones. While Canfield was in charge and the on-the-ground presence for the stores, Yellow Banana also consisted of three other members — co-founders Michael Nance, Walker Brumskine and Ademola Adewale-Sadik, all of whom did not respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Yellow Banana was pitched to Chicagoans in 2022 as a Black-owned company that wanted to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2024/05/29/save-a-lot-yellow-banana-grocery-stores-delays-south-side-gresham" target="_blank" ><u>reinvest in Save A Lot locations</u></a> that came with a reputation for dirty stores, a rat infestation and expired foods.</p><p>Yellow Banana’s legal trouble started soon after its 2021 inception, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2023/12/6/23990961/yellow-banana-ohio-sued-unpaid-bill-sells-florida-save-a-lot-stores-canfield-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>shrinking</u></a> from 38 stores across five states to the six covered under the redevelopment agreement and a seventh in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/5/11/23720073/englewood-save-a-lot-opens-at-former-whole-foods-site-without-fanfare" target="_blank" ><u>Englewood</u></a>, which is also in danger of closing Saturday. Since the deal, Canfield was also personally hit with lawsuits, liens and foreclosures.</p><p>Citations and penalties for expired foods, upcharging customers and overgrown weeds continued throughout the entirety of Yellow Banana’s ownership.</p><p>But even so, residents were overjoyed at the opening of the stores. For many, it meant they did not have to travel miles out of their way to get groceries and fresh food. <b></b></p><p>In 2024, Save A Lot stepped in to take the reins on many of Yellow Banana’s 38 locations, with the remaining stores outside of Chicago shuttering due to poor performance.</p><p><b></b> “We’ve got a big commitment in Chicago, and we really need to be able to deliver what we said. … There’s public tax dollars there,” Canfield said in September 2024. “We take that commitment very, very seriously. So we went to Save A Lot and said, ‘Hey, for us to focus on this, we should figure out a partnership here that’s going to allow this to move forward.’” <b></b></p><p>On May 29, Griffin told the Sun-Times that Save A Lot management was “leaning in, investing additional funding and operational resources into the stores and the Yellow Banana organization to ensure these stores can continue to provide a full, fresh shopping experience across Chicago.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Yellow Banana CEO Joesph Canfield speaks during the grand opening of the West Lawn Save A Lot grocery store, 4439 W. 63rd St., in 2025. His death earlier this year triggered a potential default in the city of Chicago’s redevelopment agreement. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But one month later, Save A Lot had decided to part ways with Yellow Banana, ceasing the additional funding and resources for the stores.</p><p>Alternatives, Strazzabosco said, include finding potential investors and suppliers.</p><p>The redevelopment agreement keeps Yellow Banana on the hook to keep stores open until at least 2035. The default, or breaking of the legal agreement, means city officials could force the beleaguered company to pay back the $13 million it received from tax financing to open stores in underserved neighborhoods <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/consumer-affairs/2023/8/11/23826154/supermarkets-food-access-desert-grocers-stores-walmart-whole-foods-target" target="_blank" ><u>traditional grocers had abandoned</u></a>.</p><p><b></b> “If they’re closed, each of the stores under the redevelopment agreement must be re-occupied by a grocer within one year to avoid defaults," Strazzabosco said. The seventh store, in Englewood, has 18 months under a redevelopment agreement with Englewood Square LP.</p><p>The Englewood store, despite not being covered under the redevelopment agreement, caused protests and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/4/5/23672183/englewood-save-a-lot-opening-postponed-after-pressure-from-community" target="_blank" ><u>outcry from neighbors</u></a> ahead of the 2023 opening. Yellow Banana worked with the city to secure the location, and was given subsidized rent.</p><p>“It is known as one of the worst grocery operators, poor-quality products, less-than-fresh produce, off-brand products,” Ald. Stephanie Coleman (16th) told the Sun-Times at the time. “If you visit any of their stores you’ll see that we just deserve better.” <b></b></p><p>All locations are just in need of an operator and are ready for continued occupancy, Strazzabosco said.</p><p>“The City’s priority is for the stores to remain open with a current or new operator. If they go dark, the goal is for each building to expediently reopen with a full-service grocer,” he said in a statement. “The City is exploring every opportunity to recoup taxpayer funding, if necessary.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Lauren FitzPatrick</i></p>

entries.title: Lincoln Park bar The Dime shut down after deadly weekend shooting
entries.summary: <p>A Lincoln Park bar was shuttered Tuesday after fights spilled outside and culminated in a deadly shooting this weekend.</p><p>Ald. Timmy Knudsen (43rd) said acting police Supt. Fred Waller closed the Dime, 2263 N. Lincoln Ave., "following sustained advocacy and pressure from our office."</p><p>"In partnership with the local community, my office has pushed for further restrictions and investigation of this bar due to several years of safety incidents," Knudsen said in a statement. "I am grateful to Superintendent Waller for understanding the ongoing public safety threat of this bar, and taking the rare step of a Summary Closure Order."</p><p>Malik McCorkle, 30, was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/20/man-shot-and-killed-during-fight-in-lincoln-park-1-in-custody" target="_blank" >shot multiple times</a> around 11:45 p.m. Sunday outside of King of Cups, a nearby cocktail lounge located at 2238 N Lincoln Ave., according to police and witnesses. A person of interest was later taken into custody, and a gun was recovered. </p><p>Witnesses said the shooting happened after fights broke out inside of The Dime. An altercation eventually spilled onto the sidewalk, according to city officials and nearby business owners.</p><p>Representatives for The Dime didn't respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Dino Vulpitta, co-owner of King of Cups, said his employees told him what happened, and he insisted The Dime had inadequate security to handle a large crowd.</p><p>“They had fights in the bar, so they closed it down and rushed over 200 to 300 people out into the streets,” Vulpitta said. “My doorman called the police when he saw this all happening. We had four people from St. Louis that were paying their tabs, the tourists getting ready to leave.” </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: ESPN makes new layoffs tied to NFL Network acquistion
entries.summary: <p>ESPN is undergoing a significant round of layoffs for the first time in three years after taking over NFL Network in April.</p><p>Chairman Jimmy Pitaro said in a memo to employees Tuesday morning, obtained by The Associated Press, that most moves are the result of ESPN's acquisition of NFL Network and other league digital assets last year.</p><p>The deal was announced last August and also included NFL Fantasy and the rights to distribute the RedZone channel to cable and satellite operators. In return, the NFL got a 10% equity stake in ESPN.</p><p>It was approved by government regulators in January. NFL Network employees became part of ESPN on April 1.</p><p>"Over the past several months, we've made significant progress integrating the NFL assets that we acquired into ESPN," Pitaro wrote in the memo. "Throughout this process, we have taken the time to carefully evaluate our collective teams, resources and organizational structure to best position us for the future. As a result, we had to make some difficult decisions about job impacts that we will be communicating today.</p><p>"While most of the job impacts are tied to the acquisition, we will also notify colleagues in other parts of the company today that their positions have been impacted. We are committed to treating employees with compassion and respect and to providing support as they navigate this transition."</p><p>While most of the layoffs affect production and behind-the-scenes personnel, some on-air talent were affected. Ryan Clark, who joined ESPN in 2015 as an NFL analyst, learned of his layoff while on "NFL Live" on Monday. A person familiar with the situation said Clark was originally going to be told Tuesday morning before reports leaked about the decision.</p><p>Clark was told by company executives rather than hear about it elsewhere. He did not finish his appearance on the show.</p><p>The person spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because they were not at liberty to discuss personnel decisions.</p><p>Clark took to social media on Tuesday to address the layoffs. He also shared a video of himself working out.</p><p>"Sending prayers and love to all those laid off today by ESPN. So many of you have poured your life into that company, & I know how you're feeling right now," Clark wrote on X. "My hope is as this door closes another opens for you all. God bless!"</p><p>Other notable names include Karl Ravech, who had been with ESPN since 1993 and had been an integral part of its baseball coverage. Ravech was the voice of "Sunday Night Baseball" from 2022-25 before the package moved to NBC this season. He did call Monday night's game between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Philadelphia Phillies.</p><p>Tom Pelissero, who had been with NFL Network since 2017, is also part of the cuts. ESPN had recently signed NFL insiders Ian Rapoport and Adam Schefter to extensions.</p><p>The ESPN cutbacks are also part of other reductions that are taking place throughout the Walt Disney Company this week.<br></p>
