entries.title: A root canal AND rotator cuff surgery? Lucky me.
entries.summary: <p>My dentist's office called after a routine cleaning and X-ray. Could I, they wondered, come back? Tomorrow. I got the sense that if I said, "I can rush over right now," they'd reply. "Good, hurry." It was a matter of tone.</p><p>The news was bad. An enormous cavity, growing hidden beside my upper right wisdom tooth. Maybe even invading the jaw bone. Requiring a root canal and crown. I'd probably lose the wisdom tooth too.</p><p>"I like how you're so grim," I told the dentist, after he explained the situation. "It shows you care."</p><p>Two hours in the chair for the root canal. Honestly, it didn't hurt — well, my left arm did, quite a lot, fallout from my ripped-up left shoulder. Holding still for so long. I'd occasionally extend my arm, taking care not to upset a tray of tools. </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2f0000" name="module-2f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>Then there was the enforced silence. Although, being me, I still tried to speak, with a dental dam plus dental instruments in my mouth. I wanted to tell the dentist how important Chicago is to the history of fluoridation. The initial experiments were held in Evanston in 1946, with Oak Park as the control. Being a dentist, he'd be interested. </p><p>Shutting up is an art form I struggle to master.</p><p>But that isn't the most embarrassing part.</p><p>The root canal was the first act. The second was the endodontist, who created a crown to go over the afflicted tooth, shaved down to a stump.</p><p>More than three hours in that chair, including the wait while the crown was sculpted by a high-tech medical printer. When I could speak again, this is what I said:</p><p>"You know what I was thinking for the past two hours? And this will sound like I'm blowing smoke... but I was thinking about how lucky I am to have access to high quality medical care like this."</p><p>I actually said that. And I meant it. Some 100 million Americans don't routinely see a dentist, usually because of the cost. Half the world's population suffers from untreated oral diseases, according to the World Health Organization.</p><p>A reminder. You know what's much worse than having a root canal? Needing one and not getting it.</p><p>Honestly, the root canal/crown was plenty to hone my medical gratitude. But life has a way of laying it on. A couple weeks later, I went to get an MRI on the shoulder that has hurt me since I tripped and fell on a train platform in Portugal. I was hoping the doctor would say it was merely strained, perhaps prescribe the shoulder be massaged with warm healing oils while listening to whale song.</p><p>Torn rotator cuff. Which I could ignore, going to physical therapy, building up the muscles around the detached, nearly useless muscle.</p><p>Or I could have it repaired by arthroscopic surgery. Cut a few holes in my arm, poke in a camera, set some anchors in the bone, sew the muscle back in place, out in an hour. Not even a night's stay in the hospital.</p><p>However. And this is a big honking however. I have to wear my left arm in a sling, 24 hours a day. For six weeks. Lift a coffee cup, scratch my ear, and I could rip out all the surgeon's careful handiwork. The surgeon suggested I do a few months of physical therapy and see where we stood.</p><p>I surprised myself by saying, "Nah, why wait? Let's do the surgery now."</p><p>Why? First, if I'm going to go through months of rehab, why not train a good-as-new rebuilt shoulder instead of the fraying old bum one?</p><p>Here my mother helped, quite the feat, since she's been dead for over a year. But she had a foot that was twisting, and also needed complex orthopedic surgery. She refused, for all the reasons I was tempted to say no — painful, long recovery, outcome uncertain, can blunder forward with it as it is. Eventually she could barely walk, hobbling around the Whole Foods, depending on shopping carts as walkers and the kindness of strangers. Lack of mobility eventually helped kill her.</p><p>My takeaway is: don't neglect problems. Fix them. "God grant me the courage... to change the things I can." Not necessarily for now. But for 10 years from now, when I might be glad that all the muscles in my shoulder work together as a team.</p><p>Which is a long way of saying, this is my last column for at least three weeks. Maybe more. I'm sorry to leave you in the lurch, though my colleagues will keep you informed and entertained. And rest assured, as much as you'll miss me, I'll miss you more, and get back as soon as I can.</p>

entries.title: El Berwyn Eagles Club tiene un nuevo dueño. ¿Qué significa eso para la lucha libre en el área de Chicago?
entries.summary: <p>Meses después de que el conocido recinto de lucha libre <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/04/24/berwyn-eagles-club-wrestling-fight-venue-aaw-chicago" target="_blank" >dejó de albergar luchas</a>, el Club Eagles de Berwyn tiene un nuevo propietario.</p><p>La propiedad ubicada en 6309 W. 26th St. en Berwyn ha sido vendida al vecino Berwyn Auto Spa, confirmó el propietario José Tejada. El lavado de autos <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DaOnh_buxNA/?hl=en" target="_blank" >publicó un video</a> en su cuenta de Instagram que mostraba el antiguo Club Eagles con un nuevo nombre: Destino.</p><p>Según la publicación, el edificio será convertido en un espacio para eventos. El nuevo propietario y el personal del lavado de autos no respondieron a múltiples solicitudes de comentarios adicionales sobre el futuro del antiguo Club Eagles ni qué tipos de eventos planean albergar en el espacio.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ef0000" name="module-ef0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El negocio de car wash, ubicado en 6307 W. 26th St., ofrece lavado y detallado a mano. También opera un Harold's Chicken y un bar completo que ofrece cerveza y bebidas para que los clientes disfruten mientras sus vehículos son atendidos.</p><p>Sin embargo, un sitio web del espacio no lista ningún evento próximo. Los promotores de lucha libre dicen al Sun-Times que no conocen de ningún evento de lucha libre programado allí, a pesar de la historia del edificio.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> nombre de HoboBugs Moran (y es simplemente conocido como "Bugs" por la mayoría), dijo que su empresa promotora, Wrestle League, todavía está llevando a cabo sesiones de entrenamiento en el antiguo Berwyn Eagles Club.</p><p>Le dijo al Sun-Times que Tejada le informó a Wrestle League que el recinto estaría en renovación y que el promotor necesitaría encontrar un espacio alternativo para realizar sus sesiones de entrenamiento.</p><p>El promotor agregó que encontrar un lugar asequible en la misma área general para sus aproximadamente 30 estudiantes de lucha libre podría resultar difícil.</p><p>“Mi primer combate de lucha libre en Chicago fue hace unos siete años en el Eagles Club”, comentó Bugs. “Así que, sí, definitivamente es un gran golpe que nos afecta a todos”.</p><p>Anteriormente, Bugs había pagado la renta al antiguo operador del Eagles Club, Chuck Marose Sr., para usar el espacio, comentó.</p><p>Cuando se le contactó por teléfono, Marose Sr. le dijo a un reportero que no estaba interesado en hablar y que solo quería “seguir adelante”. También dijo que la sección de Berwyn de la Fraternal Order of Eagles, que anteriormente operaba el espacio, ya no existe.</p><p>La sede nacional de la Fraternal Order of Eagles no respondió de inmediato a una consulta sobre el estado de la sección de Berwyn. Un portavoz de la Oficina del Secretario del Condado de Cook confirmó en abril que la Fraternal Order of Eagles, Berwyn Airee No. 2125, era propietario.</p><p>Los fanáticos de la lucha libre dicen que el Eagles Club ofrecía precios accesibles y estacionamiento gratuito. Algunas de las estrellas más grandes de la lucha libre mundial —como Becky Lynch de la WWE, quien asistió a Columbia College de Chicago— han derramado sangre, sudor y lágrimas en el club, convirtiéndolo en un lugar fundamental para un deporte que combina atletismo, entretenimiento y, a veces, brutalidad pura.</p><p>Ante la ausencia del Eagles Club, los promotores disponen de recintos limitados para los espectáculos de lucha libre.</p><p>Los eventos recientes se han llevado a cabo en el Logan Square Auditorium, que frecuentemente alberga shows de Freelance Wrestling y House of Glory Wrestling, y en Marionette Park, 115 Bourbon, el nuevo hogar de AAW Pro.</p><p>Pero los fanáticos dicen que trasladarse a ambos lugares puede resultar difícil y que las opciones de estacionamiento en la zona son limitadas.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: The All-Stars the Sky could’ve had are coming to Chicago
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> don’t have an All-Star in 2026, but plenty of players they could have drafted or failed to keep will be in Chicago for the game.</p><p>So here’s a rundown of their biggest All-Star whiffs, ranked not by the caliber of the player, but by what each case reveals about the Sky.</p><p>Olivia Miles is the most recent and tantalizing, though not entirely their fault. Angel Reese represents the costliest breakdown. And Marina Mabrey is the OG example of what keeps going wrong for the Sky.</p><h3>3. Olivia Miles</h3><p>The No. 2 pick in the 2026 draft used to select Miles would have belonged to the Sky. It’s the pick they gave up in 2024 to snag, then fumble, Angel Reese.</p><p>Miles is having an MVP-caliber rookie season, and the Minnesota Star Tribune has deemed her the state’s most likable athlete since Kirby Puckett. In Chicago, she could have been the most likable athlete since someone people have actually heard of. </p><p>Like Michael Jordan.</p><p>So why isn’t Miles the No. 1 whiff?</p><p>Mostly because bad luck played a major role. Had Miles entered the draft in 2025, which she strongly considered, or had the Wings done what everyone now agrees they should have done in 2026 and taken Miles over Azzi Fudd, she wouldn’t be linked to the Sky.</p><p>“You have to get lucky,” Lynx head of basketball operations Cheryl Reeve admitted when discussing Miles ending up in Minnesota. “Lottery balls have to go your way.”</p><p>Beside the aw-shucks modesty from Reeve was also a bit of a flex.</p><p>“Obviously, at the 2024 draft, we wanted to take a swing at a lottery pick in 2026,” she said. “That’s what you do when you’re trying to project teams. We have people who get paid to project for us.”</p><p>Catch the subtle reminder that the Lynx have invested in number-crunching and forecasting in a way the Sky, and many other teams, have not?</p><p>Still, some credit to the Sky for identifying Reese’s potential. They saw past the conventional wisdom that her game wouldn’t translate to the pros. If Reese were playing in her third All-Star Game for the Sky, Miles would be a road not taken, not a whiff.</p><h3>2. Angel Reese</h3><p>The Sky and Reese mutually decided to part ways this offseason, leading to her trade to Atlanta.</p><p>In a vacuum, sending away one of the game’s most recognizable young stars and the league’s best rebounder for what will likely be low first-round picks will always look pretty ugly.</p><p>But there’s a world in which the surrounding moves validate the new direction. Rickea Jackson might have the talent and personality to become the face of the franchise once her ACL heals. Adding Azurá Stevens’ floor spacing has been successful. Undrafted rookie Sydney Taylor is also showing the potential to be a star.</p><p>The problem is that none of it has showed up in the Sky's record. </p><p>And in trading up for Reese, the Sky essentially leveraged their own lack of foresight. They sacrificed a pick in a loaded 2026 draft for a star they knew would be a handful, then showed little savvy in actually managing the relationship.</p><p>They fired Teresa Weatherspoon, the coach Reese called the reason she was in Chicago. They failed to move the team out of the suburban park district during her tenure. They did not provide the resources or continuity necessary to make such a major investment last.</p><p>Not to let Reese totally off the hook. Her public criticism of the roster genuinely did not fly with her teammates, and her talents were not enough to make them a winning team.</p><p>But her assessment of the organization was true, and her willingness to say it was not out of character. The Sky got what they paid for.</p><p>They sold their Olivia Miles lottery ticket to bet on a star who calls it like she sees it, and it went about as well as the Lynx projected.</p><h3>1. Marina Mabrey</h3><p>Mabrey is the original example of the Sky’s intertwining problems since the core of their 2021 championship team broke up.</p><p>They can identify and acquire talent, often by making bets on players who have not always stuck elsewhere. They just fail to build a strong enough structure around them to make Chicago different.</p><p>After a brief stint with the Sun, Mabrey has proved herself in Toronto to be the bucket former Sky coach and general manager James Wade envisioned. She tied the all-time single-game scoring record with 53 points and is shooting 39.2% from deep on 8.4 attempts per game.</p><p>Wade sacrificed a pile of draft capital to bring her in, confident he could nurture her into an All-Star. Then he left midway through the 2023 season, and Mabrey asked out midway through 2024.</p><p>She wanted to keep her full reasoning “in house,” but acknowledged that she had been brought to Chicago to play in Wade’s system, not Weatherspoon’s.</p><p>That is the trouble with changing coaches, systems and organizational direction so frequently. A player acquired for one vision can quickly find herself stranded in another.</p><p>The part that stings is that the trade itself could have worked. None of the draft capital surrendered for Mabrey amounted to anyone special, while Mabrey became an All-Star.</p><p>Which is to say: The Sky’s aggressive approach could be vindicated if they could actually retain stars.</p><p>Instead, Mabrey — like so many others — blossomed elsewhere.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: 4 beluga whales arrive at Shedd Aquarium
entries.summary: <p>Four beluga whales plucked from a shuttered Canadian marine park arrived at Shedd Aquarium early Tuesday, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/animals/2026/07/20/beluga-whales-shedd-canada-marineland-niagara-falls" >as part of an “urgent” rescue mission</a>.</p><p>Shedd officials have said that as many as 10 belugas may be coming to Chicago in the next few weeks as part of the complex mission, which involved transporting the whales in water-filled containers both by truck and airplane.</p><p>"While the whales have arrived safely, a transport effort of this magnitude is difficult, and the aquarium cautions that experts expect to learn more about the rescued belugas’ health and current condition in the coming days," Shedd announced in a news release.</p><p>All of the new arrivals are female, "chosen to move together in a sub-pod, because of their preexisting bonds with one another," Shedd officials said.</p><p>“This moment marks the next chapter for these rescued belugas,” said Dr. Karisa Tang, lead veterinarian and vice president of animal health at Shedd. “Now that they are here, the full attention of our care and veterinary teams is on getting to know these whales and providing whatever supplemental support, care, treatment, nutrition and attention we can provide to help them acclimate to their new environment.”</p><p>The whales had been living at Marineworld Canada, which has for years faced criticism that its animals were living in unsanitary conditions. The park closed to the public in 2024, and Marineworld officials, citing extreme financial difficulties, had threatened to euthanize the whales if permanent homes couldn't be found. </p><p>Caitlin Faught, in town from Kansas City, Mo., with her family, had seen an article about Marineland closing last week. They found out some belugas were coming to the Shedd on the day they visited the aquarium, though the whales weren't ready to be seen by visitors yet.</p><p>“We saw a beluga whale!” Faught’s 4-year-old son told the Sun-Times, clutching a beluga whale stuffed animal.</p><p>While they missed the debut of the new belugas, Faught and her family felt the excitement.</p><p>“I think it's a great opportunity for them,” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1c0000" entries.title: Nine years for smuggling people from Mexico to Highland Park, turning them into 'indentured servants'
entries.summary: <p>A federal judge<b> </b>on<b> </b>Tuesday<b> </b>gave<b> </b>a<b> </b>nine-year<b> </b>prison<b> </b>sentence<b> </b>to<b> </b>a<b> </b>woman<b> </b>who<b> </b>admitted<b> </b>she<b> </b>helped<b> </b>illegally<b> </b>smuggle<b> </b>people<b> </b>into<b> </b>the<b> </b>United<b> </b>States<b> </b>from<b> </b>Mexico, harbored<b> </b>them<b> </b>in her Highland Park home, and<b> </b>forced<b> </b>them<b> </b>to<b> </b>work<b> </b>and<b> </b>turn<b> </b>over<b> </b>their<b> </b>pay.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Robert<b> </b>Gettleman<b> </b>handed the sentence to Gladys<b> </b>Ibanez-Olea, who told him she’d “forever be asking for forgiveness.”<b> </b>However, she also seemed to deny some of the allegations she’d admitted to when<b> </b>she<b> </b>pleaded<b> </b>guilty<b> </b>earlier this year.</p><p>Assistant U.S. Attorney Elie<b> </b>Zenner<b> </b>said<b> </b>Ibanez-Olea used her role<b> </b>as<b> </b>a<b> </b>cartel<b> </b>recruiter<b> </b>“to create a cadre of indentured servants.”<b> </b>She<b> </b>“controlled every aspect of their lives,”<b> </b>restricted<b> </b>access<b> </b>to<b> </b>food<b> </b>and<b> </b>medical<b> </b>care, and<b> </b>made<b> </b>“horrifying threats”<b> </b>to keep them in line, he said.</p><p>Defense attorney Jed<b> </b>Stone<b> </b>argued Ibanez-Olea was<b> </b>also a victim — sexually assaulted and taken advantage of by<b> </b>cartel<b> </b>associates<b> </b>who<b> </b>helped<b> </b>her<b> </b>enter<b> </b>the<b> </b>United States<b> </b>as she sought medical care for her children.</p><p>But Gettleman told her, “you must have known what you were putting these people through.”</p><p>“These are terrible stories,” he said.</p><p>Ibanez-Olea pleaded<b> </b>guilty<b> </b>in<b> </b>February<b> </b>to<b> </b>human<b> </b>smuggling<b> </b>and<b> </b>forced labor, admitting to a scheme involving eight victims<b> </b>that lasted for nearly a year and a half.</p><p>It began in September 2022<b> </b>when<b> </b>Ibanez-Olea<b> </b>smuggled<b> </b>a 12-year-old child<b> </b>from Mexico<b> </b>up to Highland Park, Zenner wrote in a court filing. When<b> </b>the<b> </b>girl’s<b> </b>mother<b> </b>tried to get her back, Ibanez-Olea told the mother<b> </b>that<b> </b>she<b> </b>“owned”<b> </b>the girl, according to Zenner.</p><p>When<b> </b>the<b> </b>mother<b> </b>agreed<b> </b>to<b> </b>be<b> </b>smuggled<b> </b>into the United States<b> </b>to reunite with her daughter, Ibanez-Olea told<b> </b>her<b> </b>she<b> </b>owed<b> </b>$15,000<b> </b>for the crossing, the prosecutor said. Ibanez-Olea allegedly<b> </b>forced<b> </b>the<b> </b>daughter<b> </b>to<b> </b>serve<b> </b>as<b> </b>a<b> </b>maid<b> </b>and forced<b> </b>the<b> </b>mother<b> </b>to<b> </b>work<b> </b>multiple<b> </b>jobs<b> </b>to pay off the debt.</p><p>The other victims were “trapped”<b> </b>by Ibanez-Olea in a similar manner, Zenner wrote. To keep them in her home, she<b> </b>allegedly<b> </b>took<b> </b>their<b> </b>Mexican<b> </b>identification<b> </b>documents<b> </b>and gave them fake Social Security cards.</p><p>She charged her victims for<b> </b>rent, food and utilities, and even to use a refrigerator or television, Zenner wrote. She<b> </b>refused<b> </b>to<b> </b>allow<b> </b>a<b> </b>sick<b> </b>2-year-old<b> </b>to be taken<b> </b>to a hospital, and she splashed<b> </b>cold water<b> </b>on<b> </b>a<b> </b>toddler<b> </b>to keep him<b> </b>awake<b> </b>during the day<b> </b>so he would sleep<b> </b>at night, Zenner told the judge.</p><p>It all came to an end after<b> </b>one of her victims<b> </b>escaped<b> </b>and went to the police, the prosecutor wrote. Ibanez-Olea originally faced charges in state court<b> </b>in Lake County<b> </b>before a federal grand jury handed up an indictment<b> </b>in March 2025.</p><p>Ibanez-Olea has been in custody for more than two years, so Gettleman’s sentence likely puts her on track for release some time in late 2031.</p><p>Stone wrote in his own court filing that Ibanez-Olea<b> </b>came to the United States<b> </b>seeking medical care for<b> </b>her<b> </b>two young sons. He said she was smuggled into the country<b> </b>by men associated with Mexican cartels who<b> </b>“violently raped”<b> </b>her.</p><p>She wound up working with them “out of fear,”<b> </b>Stone wrote.</p><p>Ibanez-Olea also spoke to the judge Tuesday, telling him that “a mother is capable of anything for her children. I would even give my life for them.”</p><p>But she also denied allegations made during the hearing by a victim who told the judge about the trauma she’d endured with her young child. The victim said a “simple sorry”<b> </b>wouldn’t be enough to undo it.</p><p>The victim then turned to face Ibanez-Olea in the courtroom, saying she feels “like the worst mom”<b> </b>because of what her child had been through.</p><p>“I can say that I forgive you for what you did to me,” the woman told Ibanez-Olea. “But I will never forgive you for what you did to my baby. He was a baby.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2024/02/14/highland-park-gladys-olea-trafficking-mexico-labor-onwentsia" >Highland Park woman charged with trafficking immigrants from Mexico, forcing them into labor</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: New injuries, moves for fill-in help show Cubs still desperate for pitching as trade deadline nears
entries.summary: <p>You could probably hear Trent Thornton breathing his sigh of relief on the other side of Lake Michigan.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs’</a> righty reliever came out of Monday night’s game after taking a 109-mile-an-hour liner off his foot, but Tuesday, the news seems good, that he’ll likely need just a few days to get back on the mound.</p><p>With the team’s bullpen already riddled with injuries, he didn’t want to be another.</p><p>“I do not want to go on the IL at all,” Thornton said Tuesday. “Whatever I need to do, put a Band-Aid on it, I’ll be good.</p><p>“I’m willing it that it’s going to feel fine and be good to go by later this week.”</p><p>Thornton, with a 2.70 ERA in 30 innings, has been one of several Cubs pitchers to step into unexpected roles while the staff has faced an avalanche of injuries that has threatened to bury the team.</p><p>The Cubs were thrilled they weathered the storm enough to finish the first half in playoff position.</p><p>But those clouds have not passed.</p><p>Earlier Monday, righty Phil Maton’s inflamed knee sent him to the IL for the third time this season. He’ll be out a while, with manager Craig Counsell saying Tuesday that Maton faces three weeks of inactivity after receiving a platelet-rich plasma injection.</p><p>Maton signed a two-year deal as part of Jed Hoyer’s attempt to build a strong bullpen for the second straight winter. To this point, those efforts have been far less successful than they were in 2025, with Maton’s lack of production — he’s got a 6.18 ERA — among the culprits.</p><p>Other signees, like lefty Hoby Milner (appendectomy) and righty Hunter Harvey (triceps inflammation), have been sidelined for long stretches. Righty closer Daniel Palencia is also down, in Arizona working back from elbow inflammation.</p><p>The Cubs have done great work making up for those absences from within. Thornton, lefty Ryan Rolison and righty Jacob Webb have been surprise contributors late in games.</p><p>But Hoyer, too, has searched high and low for any arms that might help shoulder the load: in-season trades for righties Tyler Ferguson and Jayden Murray and lefty David Peterson, a waiver claim on since-DFA’d righty Bryse Wilson and reunions with lefty Drew Pomeranz (also recently DFA’d) and righty Aaron Civale, just arrived in a trade with the A’s.</p><p>The Cubs, for all their work in piecing together a staff, are still desperate for pitching.</p><p>“From a pitching-staff standpoint, it’s been a challenge, obviously, with all the injuries,” Hoyer said last week. “That’s been challenging to get to steady footing, so to speak, and … the hope is we can get to that place.</p><p>“We may seek that out the entire [rest of the season], but to be in a place where we have more stability, pitching-wise, would be wonderful.”</p><p>While the minor moves, like the Civale trade, could help the Cubs survive, they figure to need something bigger to position themselves as true contenders alongside the Dodgers and Brewers on the NL side of the playoff bracket.</p><p>Might that mean pursuing a big-time starter? Or just more of Counsell’s beloved “out-getters”?</p><p>“Craig likes out-getters. He also likes not burning through the bullpen all the time,” Hoyer said a few days before Counsell used eight pitchers in Monday’s loss. “It’s important to be able to give him some stability.</p><p>“[One guy] getting 18 or even 21 outs in a game makes the next game a lot easier. … It has a cascading impact that is real. Of course, that would be important.”</p><p>Tarik Skubal is in the opposing dugout during this week’s series at Wrigley Field. Whether the Tigers end up parting with the superstar lefty, a back-to-back Cy Young winner, at the deadline remains to be seen. Whether the Cubs have the prospect capital to compete for his services is also a question.</p><p>Who else? Marlins righty Sandy Alcantara? Angels lefty Reid Detmers? Blue Jays righty Kevin Gausman? Red Sox righty Sonny Gray? Mets righty Clay Holmes? Tigers righty Casey Mize? Twins righty Joe Ryan?</p><p>And that’s without mentioning any relievers.</p><p>The logistics of any deal go well beyond need. But when it comes to filling the Cubs’ need, they all fit the bill.</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-c90005" name="list-c90005"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, pageNumber=1, titleUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs, inverseColors=false, footerBgColor=#000000, title=Latest on the Cubs, bodyFont=font-3, showListNumbers=false, imagePositionHorizontal=null, rteBodyFont=font-3, headerBottomBorderColor=#111010, subTitle=null, stickyHeader=true, listTitleColor=#000000, tableCellBorderColor=#ccd1d5, relatedListFont=font-1, hideAuthors=true, tertiaryTextColor=#6c6c6c, buttonHoverTextColor=#ffffff, tableFont=font-1, carouselAutoPlay=false, promoTitleFont=font-2, ctaButtonText=[], primaryTextColor=#2a2a2a, buttonTextColor=#ffffff, linkTextColor=#1a1a1a, hideTitles=false, footerLinkColor=#ffffff, count=14107, pagination=[{body=[Next Page], href=?p=2, _template=/link/Link.hbs, contentId=null, pianoSectionSlug=null, target=null}], items=[{type=Image, url=https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/20/chicago-cubs-jameson-taillon-craig-counsell-phil-maton-drew-pomeranz-aaron-civale-daniel-palencia, categoryUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs, publishDate=July 20, 2026 09:05 PM, wordCount=768, _styledTemplate=null, description=[{items=[Taillon allowed a three-run homer to Riley Greene and a solo shot to Dillon Dingler to put the Cubs in an early hole. entries.title: Women suffer more severe neurologic symptoms from long COVID than men, researchers find
entries.summary: <p>New research from Northwestern Medicine showed for the first time that women suffer more severe neurologic symptoms due to long COVID, such as brain fog and numbness, than men.</p><p>The research, published Tuesday in the <a class="Link" href="https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/acn3.70468" target="_blank" ><u>Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology</u></a>, also found that women with long COVID experienced worse effects on their quality of life and cognitive functioning than men.</p><p>The research is based on evaluations of 2,329 patients who sought care at Northwestern’s COVID clinic during a five-year period from May 2020 through August 2025. Women reported experiencing more neurologic symptoms than men, about 16 months, on average, from when the symptoms first started, according to the journal article. Some of the most common neurologic symptoms include brain fog, numbness, dizziness, tinnitus or ringing or buzzing in the ear, blurred vision and muscle pain.</p><p>Patients completed quality-of-life surveys in which women reported higher levels of fatigue than men, leading to a decrease in daily activities. Women also reported experiencing more non-neurologic symptoms than men, like shortness of breath, chest pain and dysautonomia, or a group of diseases that affect the automatic functions of the body, such as heart rate or digestion, according to the study. Women also scored lower than men in a task of attention on cognitive tests.</p><p>Dr. Igor Koralnik, who heads neuroinfectious diseases at Northwestern Medicine, was among those who authored the research. Their findings are significant, he said, because researchers knew more women were experiencing long COVID — they make up about two-thirds of Northwestern’s COVID clinic — but now they also know that women are more severely affected than men. That’s particularly important because there are millions living with long COVID across the country.</p><p>“You don’t have people hospitalized with terrible pneumonia dying in the hospital,” Koralnik said. “On the other hand, you have a silent epidemic that continues with long COVID, and since people have moved on in a sense from COVID-19, they are forgetting that people still have long COVID.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b30000" name="image-b30000"></a> <picture class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Grace Huffman-Gottschling, who has had long COVID since 2022, near her home at Horner Park in Chicago. She’s had to change how she lives her life to budget her limited energy.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>For Grace Huffman-Gottschling, the fatigue from long COVID has meant she isn’t swimming like she used to before she got sick four years ago. Everyday tasks like cooking, cleaning or shopping also look different now.</p><p>“I sort of have to budget my energy day in and day out, and a lot of that has to be prioritized toward making a living,” Huffman-Gottschling said. “I just don’t have tons of capacity for other things.”</p><p>Huffman-Gottschling, 28, of the Irving Park neighborhood, got sick with COVID in April 2022, though she suspects she could have gotten it earlier when her family got sick. In the summer of 2022, she went to Northwestern after she was still experiencing symptoms from COVID like shortness of breath and chest pain.</p><p>An inhaler, which she occasionally still uses, helped alleviate the shortness of breath. She also underwent cognitive rehabilitation to reduce brain fog, which did initially help. Huffman-Gottschling has also participated in studies related to long COVID.</p><p>Her health has felt stagnant as she continues experiencing chronic fatigue, brain fog and gastrointestinal symptoms.</p><p>“There’s sort of these lingering neurological things and other things that still make day-to-day pretty tough,” Huffman-Gottschling said.</p><p>Researchers already knew that women, in particular those younger and middle-age, were experiencing long COVID more than men, Koralnik said. Because of their genetic predisposition, women are better at fighting acute infection, meaning their mortality rates tend to be lower, he said. But that also means that women are more prone to get autoimmune diseases, and Koralnik said scientists believe long COVID is a new autoimmune disease.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> Osorio/Northwestern Medicine</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Sometimes patients become symptomatic immediately after the first episode of long COVID; sometimes it’s after the second, third or fourth episode,” Koralnik said. “It’s as if you have a river where the water level goes up and up to the point that the river goes over the dam and then floods the system.”</p><p>Huffman-Gottschling had lived with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, also known as POTS, for years before getting sick with COVID. She initially thought her symptoms were tied to the chronic condition.</p><p>But now, she finds herself juggling multiple conditions, which means her schedule is usually filled with medical appointments. She describes the research, like Tuesday’s study on the disparate impact on women, important to help others understand how COVID continues to affect people like her.</p><p>“It’s a condition that … can be very wide-ranging in terms of symptoms and impact, is very, very hard on people,” Huffman-Gottschling said. “And there’s still not always clear treatments that help alleviate symptoms for so many of us who’ve been experiencing symptoms for years and years at this point.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2025/03/21/doctors-patients-battle-long-covid-five-years-on" >Long COVID remains a battle for patients, doctors alike five years post-lockdown</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/01/17/northwestern-study-of-long-covid-patients-shows-how-an-app-can-track-recovery" >Northwestern study of long COVID patients shows how an app can track recovery</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Former Chicago Daily News building now a city landmark
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Daily News building opened 97 years ago, helping to establish the city as a center for media and architecture.</p><p>Although the Daily News moved out of the 26-story, steel-framed riverfront building in 1960, the structure's importance never diminished.</p><p>Last week, the City Council designated the Art Deco skyscraper at 2 N. Riverside Plaza as an official Chicago landmark.</p><p>“It's a building that was incredibly important for a number of reasons: architecturally but also urbanistically and culturally to the city. Because of where it is and what is across the river from it, it never really has received the kind of star treatment that it deserves,” Thomas Leslie, the Ralph E. Johnson professor of design at the Illinois School of Architecture at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said. “It’s great to see it getting landmarked, and probably long overdue.”</p><p>According to the city, the Near West Side building is undergoing a nearly $70 million commercial rehabilitation by the owner, 2 N. Riverside Owner LLC.</p><p>The building, designed by Holabird & Root, was completed in 1929. It was the first office structure in the city built above railroad tracks and the first with a public plaza.</p><p>Leslie said the landmark designation is due not only to the building’s importance to journalism in Chicago but also its design.</p><p>“It’s a really important piece of urbanism. It was one of the first buildings in the city to face the river, which for a long time had just been an industrial sewer. It’s an important piece of the Downtown landscape in that it's a building that really does try to connect the city with the riverfront, and that's a tradition that goes on today,” Leslie said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-9d0000" name="image-9d0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/be02ca7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F26%2F49%2F911773f04e4e83c2073a1e6b5634%2Fnews-260402-8.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5d08689/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F26%2F49%2F911773f04e4e83c2073a1e6b5634%2Fnews-260402-8.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6d07a13/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F26%2F49%2F911773f04e4e83c2073a1e6b5634%2Fnews-260402-8.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Some of the Art Deco architectural details on the former Chicago Daily News building at 2 N. Riverside Plaza, photographed March 31, 2026." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6d07a13/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F26%2F49%2F911773f04e4e83c2073a1e6b5634%2Fnews-260402-8.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/49735c5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F26%2F49%2F911773f04e4e83c2073a1e6b5634%2Fnews-260402-8.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6d07a13/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F26%2F49%2F911773f04e4e83c2073a1e6b5634%2Fnews-260402-8.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Some of the Art Deco architectural details on the former Chicago Daily News building, at 2 N. Riverside Plaza.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Design and engineering praised</h3><p>The building’s design is considered Art Deco, though Leslie prefers "streamlined moderne."</p><p>“It’s a style that was very much kind of looking to both classical architecture but also to modernism. A lot of the ornament is really stripped down and abstracted,” Leslie said. “It shows that kind of moment where architectural tastes were really changing. It opens up this beautiful plaza to the riverfront.”</p><p>The structure also is a marvel of structural engineering, Leslie said.</p><p>“It was built on top of the active rail yards that were west of the Loop, and the structure is literally woven down through the tracks which were existing at the time. You can't see any of that steelwork but it held up all of the newspaper’s printing presses, literally suspended over the tracks when it opened,” Leslie said. “It’s really an important landmark for its engineering prowess, in addition to its style. This is a building that encapsulates so much about what the city is all about, how the city relates to the river, its history with writing, with journalism, and then also, if you look really closely, its really long history with structural engineering.”</p><p>The Daily News was founded in 1875 by Melville Stone. Under the leadership of publisher Victor Lawson, it earned a reputation for journalistic integrity and innovation.</p><p>Lawson died in 1925, four years before the Daily News moved into its new building. The newspaper was home to such journalism luminaries as Eugene Field, Carl Sandburg, Ben Hecht, Peter Lisagor and Mike Royko. The paper pioneered foreign news services. It was the first Chicago newspaper to win a Pulitzer Prize and over the years won 13 in all. It also established radio station WMAQ in 1922, then sold it to NBC in 1931.</p><h3>The end of the Daily News</h3><p>In 1959, the Daily News was purchased by the Chicago Sun-Times, and Daily News staffers moved into the Sun-Times' building at 401 N. Wabash Ave. That building was demolished 2004; the site is now home to Trump Tower.</p><p>Former Chicago Sun-Times reporter and editor Scott Fornek got his start in 1977 as a Daily News copy boy at the Wabash building. By then, the Daily News, an afternoon paper, was nearing its end.</p><p>“I worked less than six months for the Daily News, and then I was out of work for a while. Then in the summer of 1978, I was rehired by the Sun-Times,” said Fornek, 67, who retired last year.</p><p>Though he never worked in the Riverside Plaza building, Fornek said its landmark status is well-deserved.</p><p>“I think it’s a good thing. Chicago is a great newspaper town. It’s still a great journalism town, but in the days of newspapers, it was a great newspaper town," Fornek said.</p><p>"There was a time when there were like six or seven papers, morning and daily papers. The Daily News was part of that history.”</p><p>Ward Miller, executive director of the nonprofit Preservation Chicago, said the designation for the building is the result of a nearly 20-year effort.</p><p>“The old Chicago Daily News building was one of our most endangered buildings," Miller said. “We're hoping that this landmark designation really does bring a spotlight to this building that it protects it in perpetuity and it encourages a reinvestment in this structure.”</p><p><i>Michael Puente is a reporter and anchor for WBEZ. Reach him at </i><a class="Link" href="mailto:mpuente@wbez.org" target="_blank" ><i><u>mpuente@wbez.org</u></i></a><i>.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/04/01/chicago-daily-news-building-landmark-status" >Former Chicago Daily News building could be in line for landmark status</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/architecture/2026/04/21/whats-that-building-mural-from-the-old-daily-news-building" target="_blank" >WBEZ: Historic 1929 mural from old Daily News building still in storage</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Gazpacho with a cocktail twist is a satisfying antidote to a warm day
entries.summary: <p>In the heat of summer, it’s best to keep meals light and fresh. Cold soups and leafy salads step up to the main course, providing clean and refreshing nourishment, while taking advantage of the bounty of the garden and farmers markets.</p><p>Gazpacho is a satisfying antidote to a warm day. It’s a chilled tomato soup of Spanish origin that's unfailingly refreshing in the heat. This recipe veers from the traditional blended version and looks to a shrimp cocktail for further inspiration. Instead of pureeing the ingredients, it calls for chopping and dicing the vegetables, which provide wholesome crunch and texture to the soup. (Yes, it takes more time, but it’s worth the effort.) The diced vegetables swim and mingle in the tomato juice, imparting a medley of sweetness, heat and crunch to every bite — or slurp, as it were.</p><p>The soup’s tomato juice base is infused with cocktail sauce ingredients, including horseradish, lemon and Worcestershire sauce. Poached and chilled shrimp are draped around the rim of the glass, evoking a shrimp cocktail, providing protein and more substance and an excuse to call this soup a main course. It’s a colorful and dramatic bowl, served as a light and vibrant main dish or divided between small glasses as an appetizer.</p><h3>Shrimp Cocktail Gazpacho</h3><p><b>Yield:</b> Serves 4 to 6</p><p><b>Ingredients</b></p><p><b>Soup:</b></p><p>4 cups unseasoned tomato juice<br>1 pint grape or cherry tomatoes, chopped<br>1 English cucumber, seeded, diced (with skin)<br>1 small red onion, finely chopped<br>1 large celery stalk, diced<br>1 medium red bell pepper, stemmed and seeded, diced<br>1 small poblano pepper, stemmed and seeded, diced<br>1 large garlic clove, grated<br>1/4 cup fresh lemon juice<br>2 tablespoons fresh lime juice<br>1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil<br>2 teaspoons drained prepared horseradish, or to taste<br>1 to 2 teaspoons Worcestershire sauce<br>1 teaspoon hot sauce, such as Tabasco<br>3/4 teaspoon kosher salt, or more to taste<br>1/2 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper<br>1/4 cup chopped flat-leaf parsley or cilantro leaves</p><p><b>Shrimp:</b><br>1 pound jumbo (16/18) shrimp, peeled and deveined, tails intact<br>Juice of 1/2 lemon<br>1 medium yellow onion, quartered<br>1 tablespoon kosher salt<br>1 teaspoon black peppercorns<br>Celery stalks and lime or lemon wedge, for garnish</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Combine all the soup ingredients, except the parsley or cilantro, in a large bowl. Stir to blend, and taste for seasoning. Cover the soup and refrigerate for at least 2 hours or up to 6 hours to chill and allow the flavors to develop.</p><p>While the soup is chilling, poach the shrimp. Fill a large saucepan with water. Add the lemon juice, onion, salt and peppercorns. Bring to a boil over high heat. Remove the pan from the heat and add the shrimp. Cover the pot and let stand until the shrimp turn pink and are just opaque through the center, about 4 minutes. Drain the shrimp and rinse under cold water to stop the cooking process. Refrigerate until use.</p><p>Remove the gazpacho from the refrigerator 10 to 15 minutes before serving. Stir in the parsley or cilantro and taste again for seasoning. Ladle the soup into glasses or small bowls and drape the shrimp around the edges. Serve garnished with a lemon or lime wedge or a celery stalk.</p><p><i>Lynda Balslev is an award-winning writer, cookbook author and recipe developer, and authors the blog TasteFood.</i></p>

entries.title: Chicago cop on Ald. Dowell's security team charged with attacking his child's mother
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago cop tasked with protecting a top City Council leader was charged this week with battering the mother of his child, months after she was granted a protective order following another alleged attack.</p><p>Officer Roderick Hummons, 49, was stripped of his police powers and ordered to hand over his weapons after he was charged Monday with a misdemeanor count of domestic battery, according to court records and the police department.</p><p>Hummons is accused of choking and hitting his child’s mother at his apartment on the Near West Side, according to an arrest report obtained by the Sun-Times. Officers said she had visible bruising and cuts on her face.</p><p>Hummons was assigned to Unit 544, which handles security for city officials, including Mayor Brandon Johnson.</p><p>A spokesperson for Ald. Pat Dowell, chair of the powerful Finance Committee, said Hummons worked on her security detail and has now been removed. Dowell’s spokesperson noted that Hummons and other officers are regularly rotated among city officials’ security teams.</p><p>Hummons’ attorney, Tim Grace, denied the allegations, saying his client “did not engage in the alleged activity.”</p><p>Grace said they “looked forward” to fighting the charges in court.</p><p>He was taken into custody early Monday after officers responded to a report of a domestic disturbance at his home. The woman’s mother had called 911 after she witnessed Hummons attacking her daughter during a FaceTime call, according to the arrest report.</p><p>Hummons told responding officers that his child’s mother had doused him in baby oil while he was sleeping, the report says. He said the woman had also struck him and cut his ear.</p><p>She told police that she poured oil on him because she suspected he had been cheating on her with a neighbor, according to the report. Hummons then got up and began choking her and punching her in the face, the woman said.</p><p>Her mother told officers that she saw the attack over the video call, the report says. But the mother of Hummons' child refused to sign a domestic battery complaint. Instead, an officer signed the complaint and took Hummons into custody.</p><p>He was released after a court hearing Monday and was ordered to stay away from the woman, records show. </p><p>It wasn’t the first time.</p><p>Hummons' child’s mother previously filed for an order of protection on April 6, saying she had been arrested after Hummons falsely accused her of making a violent threat to take custody of their child. Court records indicate that criminal case was dropped.</p><p>In her petition for the protective order, the woman said Hummons was “mentally abusive” and “very controlling.” She noted she “had several physical altercations” and was once sent to the hospital with “a jaw injury.”</p><p>“I fear for my life because of his emotional rampages,” she wrote.</p><p>The order of protection was granted and Hummons was ordered to stay away from the woman. But within days, she moved to have the order vacated.</p><p>“Roderick and I have a 2 year old daughter and I wish to vacate the order of protection so we can parent our child together. I’ll also love to work this out without the court involvement,” she told a judge on April 10.</p><p>Court records show the order of protection was cleared on April 21.</p><p>Hummons was expected in court again on Aug. 11 in the battery case.</p><p>The security unit he worked on was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2022/3/28/22985559/mayor-lightfoot-security-dozens-chicago-cops-guard-mayor-family-below-radar-security-unit" target="_blank" >created in 2020</a> to protect then-Mayor Lori Lightfoot’s home and City Hall and oversee her personal detail. It began with just a handful of Chicago police officers, but by 2022 grew to include 65 officers, five sergeants and a lieutenant.</p><p>As of June, he was among 95 members working in Unit 544.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2022/3/28/22985559/mayor-lightfoot-security-dozens-chicago-cops-guard-mayor-family-below-radar-security-unit" target="_blank" >Dozens of Chicago cops guard mayor and family in below-the-radar security unit created in 2020</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2026/06/03/david-ross-larry-snelling-chicago-police-cpd-copa" target="_blank" >Chicago cop faces firing after passing test to join horseback unit while sidelined with ‘unbearable’ injury</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2026/06/25/chicago-police-cpd-diana-valentine-revenge-porn" target="_blank" >Pregnant Chicago police officer posted revenge porn after catching kid’s father cheating, records show</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Leahy Building in River North, home to Sound Bar nightclub, sold for conversion to apartments
entries.summary: <p>A largely vacant River North building has been sold to a local real estate investment firm that plans to convert the building into apartments.</p><p>Concord Capital purchased the building at 226 W. Ontario St. for about $4.1 million, according to Drew Millard, principal of the firm. The private sale closed July 14.</p><p>Prior to the sale, the building was owned by Onrio Management Corp. As of Tuesday, the management firm was still advertising the building as for sale on <a class="Link" href="https://www.onriomanagement.com/our-space" target="_blank" >its website</a>, pitching 226 W. Ontario as “[combining] the sturdy elegance of early 20th-century design with the conveniences of today.”</p><p>Crain’s Chicago Business reported that <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagobusiness.com/real-estate/commercial/ccb-226-west-ontario-street-conversion-20260720/" target="_blank" >the late Michael Wellek</a>, the owner and operator of several adult entertainment clubs in the Chicago suburbs, was tied to Onrio.</p><p>Concord plans to turn the structure, also known as the Leahy Building, into 70 apartments, with 10 of them in a two-story addition atop the building’s existing structure. Those residences will include private outdoor spaces, Millard said, in addition to rooftop terraces.</p><p>The building’s occupancy was “very low” prior to the sale, said CBRE Vice President Dominic Soltero, who represented the seller. The nightclub Sound Bar — also owned by Wellek before his passing — operates on the building’s lower floors.</p><p>Millard said the nightclub, where a security guard <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/3/22/18438102/sound-bar-security-guard-was-killed-during-shoot-out-with-patrons-prosecutors" >died in 2019</a> after a shoot-out between patrons, will vacate the building in eight months, but the firm plans to begin construction prior to that. Sound Bar is in the building’s basement, Millard said, and that coupled with the nightclub’s operating hours mean it shouldn’t be impacted by the construction.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The Leahy Building stands at six stories and 48,000 square feet, and the new development will include a mix of studios, one-bedroom and two-bedroom units upon completion. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Millard said Sound Bar being the only current tenant is a huge boon for the firm. One of the many difficulties of converting an office building can be navigating the leases of existing tenants. Oftentimes, a building needs to be vacated before demolition and interior work can begin.</p><p>Millard said the firm was also attracted to the Leahy Building for its prime River North location and size. Many office buildings don’t work for residential because the floors are too wide, Millard said, which limits how many windows can be put in each unit.</p><p>Concord plans to call the residential building Leahy Lofts. The building stands at six stories and 48,000 square feet and will include a mix of studios, one-bedroom and two-bedroom units upon completion. One-bedroom units with dens will also be available.</p><p>The basement already has some lounge space built out because of Sound Bar, but Millard said he isn’t sure if his firm will use it or not. The basement will house multiple amenities, such as a gym, resident lounge, coworking center and bike storage room.</p><p>The Leahy Building joins an emerging pipeline of River North office buildings that are going residential. Concord is finishing up the conversion of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/07/31/developer-convert-river-north-office-shoe-factory-apartments" >223 W. Erie St.</a>, which is next door to the Leahy Building. And, in May, Path Construction and WindWave Real Estate welcomed the first residents at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/04/10/former-salesforce-office-residents-river-north-building-apartments" >111 Point</a>, the former Salesforce office building in River North.</p><p>Concord is working on nine office-to-residential conversions in Chicago, Millard said. The projects span from River North and Streeterville to one in Printers Row.</p><p>Despite the limited number of buildings available for conversion, Millard believes more projects will join the conversion pipeline over the next two years.</p><p>“The competition is definitely stepping up. However, there's only so many office buildings to convert,” Millard said. “We've got our eye on a bunch of others, but this isn’t going to last five years because we'll run out of them.”</p><p>CBRE’s private capital and land services team has completed six office-to-residential conversion deals in the past year, according to the firm. Soltero said many of those deals are in neighborhoods like River North and Streeterville, where some companies are fleeing for trendier business corridors in Fulton Market and West Loop. But demand to live close to downtown is still there, and he said more conversions can help meet it.</p><p>“The young generation still wants to live in a very live, work, play atmosphere,” Soltero said. "It's very lively [in River North], and it's getting better and better."</p><p>The $20 million project is being privately funded and doesn’t require the city to sign off on a zoning change, Millard said. The firm hopes to break ground in October after demolition and complete the project in spring 2028.</p>

entries.title: Chicago police set directives for collecting evidence on ICE agents suspected of breaking the law
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police have finally issued guidelines on how to collect and retain evidence against federal immigration agents suspected of violating state law, six months after a mayoral executive order directing them to do so.</p><p>Much of the new guidance refers to existing department policies, and clarifies that regular police work, such as rendering medical aid and using body cameras, shouldn’t stop — even if federal agents are considered crime suspects.</p><p>Police are directed to record incidents involving immigration officers using their body-worn cameras, and to identify the names of top federal agents at a scene. The guidance also specifies the formal channels officers should use to receive, document and potentially investigate complaints made against the feds.</p><p>Spelling out that responsibility for officers, even if it was already baked into existing protocol, was a key goal of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/01/31/brandon-johnson-investigate-ice-prosecution-executive-order-chicago" >Mayor Brandon Johnson’s executive order.</a></p><p>The Chicago Police Department didn’t immediately respond to questions about training officers have received or will receive on the new guidance.</p><p>WBEZ reporting revealed that the executive order had not been formally implemented despite a February deadline. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/17/ice-midway-blitz-chicago-police-brandon-johnson" >At a City Council hearing Friday, </a>alderpersons grilled police officials about the delays.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/15/brandon-johnson-city-council-ice-immigration-midway-blitz" >Mayor Johnson’s plan to crack down on ICE agents under City Council scrutiny</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>In March, Johnson told reporters that a new policy wasn’t needed to implement the executive order. But last week, a spokesperson told WBEZ that guidance was still under development.</p><p>Johnson’s executive order has stirred confusion since its inception, namely because of a clause that required officers to refer felony matters to Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke “at the direction of the Mayor’s Office.” O’Neill Burke slammed that requirement as “wholly inappropriate.”</p><p>The new guidance doesn’t name the mayor’s office. Instead, it clarifies that incidents “will continue to be investigated and referred to the Cook County State's Attorney consistent with the existing Department directives.”</p><p>Last week, the mayor’s office walked back that language in a statement, saying it hasn’t reviewed or consulted on any potential referrals for criminal charges to the state’s attorney since the order was signed.</p><p>“The Mayor’s Office’s role is to establish that policy direction, not to review, oversee, or participate in individual investigations or referral decisions,” a spokesperson said.</p><p>Immigrant advocates who want to see the executive order enforced point to a recent, high-profile<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/02/federal-agents-crash-into-car-while-detaining-man-in-albany-park" > incident in Albany Park</a> in which an ICE agent crashed an SUV into a woman’s car and fled before police arrived.</p><p>Pooja Ravindran, the chief of staff for the Council’s Committee on Immigration and Refugee Rights, said this is the type of case that could be investigated and potentially referred for criminal prosecution. Instead, officers simply “clocked it as a traffic incident” because that’s how witnesses characterized it, Ravindran said.</p><p>The executive order also requires officers to “publicly report aggregated data” on incidents involving federal immigration agents.</p><p>The new guidance directs officers to log complaints by members of the public under a category titled “Apparent Violation of Law by Federal Law Enforcement.”</p><p>It’s unclear how the police department plans to report that data publicly.</p>

entries.title: New Ryan Field gives Northwestern a spectacular football venue 100 years in the making
entries.summary: <p>In 1925, Northwestern briefly dreamed of building one of the largest stadiums in the nation, then did nothing of the sort.</p><p>A century later, Northwestern identified a different superlative target for its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2025/07/30/northwestern-ryan-field-wildcats-mark-jackson-david-braun-evanston-big-ten-college-football" target="_blank" >new stadium</a>. This time, the university might have achieved it.</p><p>"I truly believe it's the best stadium in all of football," Wildcats coach David Braun said Tuesday. "We're not trying to be the biggest. We delivered on being the best."</p><p>Construction is progressing rapidly on the new Ryan Field, scheduled to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/02/03/northwestern-new-ryan-field-delay" target="_blank" >open Oct. 2</a> vs. Penn State, and it's revealing a spectacular — and extremely purple — facility that evokes an English Premier League venue more than a Big Ten stadium.</p><p>That soccer vibe particularly stems from two elements. One is a 360-degree roof designed to shield all 35,000 seats from weather and to amplify crowd noise, which Northwestern hasn't exactly been known for in the past.</p><p>The other is the standing-room-only student section behind the southern end zone, which rises steeply enough to require horizontal railings between each row. When populated, it should resemble a wall of fans on top of the field.</p><p>All around, though, it's a beautiful facility, one that looks starkly out-of-place across the street from humble three-story brick apartment buildings in Evanston but inside feels like a self-contained futuristic sporting world of its own.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The vertical student section at new Ryan Field adds to the soccer-stadium vibe.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ben Pope/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>It's especially surreal that Northwestern will now call this facility home, given the nature of old Ryan Field.</p><p>There was a certain charm to that dump, but it was a dump. The rusty metal bleachers, crumbling white concrete and jarring asymmetry between its tall western and stumpy eastern stands — the stadium's visible-on-TV features — were somehow more flattering than the dim, dirty maze of hallways underneath the stadium that fans in person traversed.</p><p>But it's perhaps less surreal with historical context. James Rogers, the old stadium's architect, <a class="Link" href="https://dailynorthwestern.com/2016/11/22/sports/football-northwestern-and-ryan-fields-near-ascendency-into-college-football-glory/" target="_blank" >initially imagined it</a> as a behemoth in the mold of Michigan Stadium, which was built around the same time.</p><p>Northwestern was a national title contender during the 1920s and early 1930s and didn't yet differ greatly in size from its peers, so Rogers' early blueprints envisioned one of the first-ever triple-decker stadiums — following the world’s first, Yankee Stadium, by only three years.</p><p>Financial constraints and realism eventually triumphed over those ambitions, and Northwestern ultimately didn't follow Notre Dame and USC into the modern-day tier of private-school blue bloods. Would an enormous stadium have changed that course? Who knows.</p><p>It's fitting, albeit probably coincidental, that the new Ryan Field does feature three decks. They create an optical illusion which makes the stadium seem larger than it actually is.</p><p>That's because each deck is relatively shallow. There's a lot of structure; there aren't a lot of seats. Behind the northern end zone, for example, the first deck contains only 12 rows of seats and the second deck only three rows.</p><p>Capacity has been reduced by more than 12,000 from the old stadium, making new Ryan Field the smallest in the Big Ten and the second-smallest in the power conferences.</p><p>That's a smart move for Northwestern considering its small, geographically dispersed and not exactly sports-obsessed alumni base. That "small" adjective cannot be emphasized enough: Northwestern's annual graduating class is less than half the size of the second-smallest Big Ten school, Nebraska.</p><p>The idea is that smaller capacity equates to a higher percentage of seats being occupied by devoted season-ticket holders, limiting opportunities for larger fan bases to take over the stadium like they used to.</p><p>Considering Northwestern hasn't even consistently packed its 15,000-seat temporary lakefront stadium the last two seasons, there's no guarantee that effort will pay off. Realistically, attendance is likely an eternal challenge for the school.</p><p>But at least Northwestern now has a stadium that will actively attract fans instead of deter them.</p>

entries.title: Loop’s arts and culture visitors contribute $395 million to the economy
entries.summary: <p>Visitors to arts and culture venues in the Loop are bringing more dollars to Downtown, but weekday foot traffic is still below 2019 levels, according to Chicago Loop Alliance’s second-quarter report released on Tuesday.</p><p>Arts and cultural events drew nearly 1.5 million visitors from April through June. They contributed more than $395 million to the local economy, representing a 20% rise compared to the second quarter last year.</p><p>Events such as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/suenos-music-festival" >Sueños Music Festival,</a> Chicago Blues Festival, Daley Plaza Farmers Market and Millennium Park’s concerts and films were popular attractions.</p><p>But like many U.S. downtowns, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/04/08/civic-leaders-chicago-loop-alliance-state-street" target="_blank" ><u>State Street</u></a> in the Loop has struggled following the COVID-19 pandemic. Since 2020, more than 15 retailers have vacated the Downtown corridor, including Anthropologie, Express, H&M and Urban Outfitters.</p><p>Efforts are underway to lure people Downtown and revive Chicago’s economic engine. In February, the Loop Alliance unveiled plans for a new <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/loop/2026/02/27/chicago-loop-alliance-arts-district-state-street-funding-vacant-stores" target="_blank" ><u>arts district</u></a>. Nearly 90 Loop arts organizations will develop the neighborhood as an arts and culture destination.</p><p>In the second quarter, high office and commercial vacancies in the Loop began to level off, Loop Alliance said. Nineteen new restaurants and cafes opened in the Loop from April to June. Twenty others recently opened or are expected to open this year. Overall, investment in new construction and renewed uses of existing Loop property totaled $673 million in the second quarter.</p><p><b></b> In February, the Loop Alliance announced it received an $800,000 two-year grant from the Department of Planning and Development to help fill vacant storefronts through community investment like preparing the empty spaces and supporting small businesses. <b></b></p><p>Office occupancy was 1% higher in April and May compared to those months in 2024 “showing that hybrid work trends are here to stay in the Loop,” Chicago Loop Alliance said in a news release. New office leases included ones from Huntington Bank and law firm Vedder Price.</p><p>Weekend pedestrians on State Street were 5% above 2019 levels. But weekday foot traffic was only about 82% of 2019 levels.</p><p>The CTA saw an average of nearly 1 million riders across all lines each weekday in the first quarter, representing an 11% increase compared to the same period last year. Crimes at all CTA locations are down by about 25% compared to this time last year, according to the CTA.</p><p><b></b> “While the Loop’s foundation as a central business district continues to thrive, we are heartened by the neighborhood’s progress transitioning to a fully activated, multi-use district — filled with vibrant arts and culture, bustling retail activity and engaged residents,” Suzet McKinney, CEO of Chicago Loop Alliance, said in a news release. <b></b></p><p>Three residential buildings are under construction as a part of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/04/14/la-salle-street-revamp-tif-district-office-to-residential-conversion-brandon-johnson-lori-lightfoot" target="_blank" ><u>LaSalle Corridor Revitalization</u></a> Initiative to convert office buildings to residences. Along with those city-funded projects, there are 19 other privately funded downtown conversions planned. Those projects will bring nearly 4,000 new residential units and over $1.67 billion in investment<b> </b>to the Loop, according to the Department of Planning and Development.</p>

entries.title: Patty García wants to move past last minute ballot maneuver, says voters 'aren't talking about the process'
entries.summary: <p>Democratic congressional candidate Patty García is hoping she can turn the page on the controversy swirling around her nomination — and petition objections that knocked two of her independent challengers off the ballot on Tuesday — to focus on issues she says are affecting the 4th Congressional District, including ongoing ICE presence and threats to reproductive rights.</p><p>And she says voters in the district aren't talking about "the process." </p><p>"What I'm hearing at the doors is people concerned about immigration following them. 'Is it safe to apply for citizenship right now? Are we going to be able to find better jobs and good jobs that don't have us questioning and rationing food versus rent?'" García told the Sun-Times on Tuesday. "So for me, listening to the voters, that's my pulse and the reality of where the community is at. And they're not talking about the process. They're talking about things that matter to them day to day."</p><p>García, who was serving as U.S. Rep. Jesus "Chuy" García's chief of staff, officially announced her candidacy in November, about nine days after both Patty García and Rep. García filed nominating petitions to run as a Democrat for the 4th Congressional District. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2025/11/03/jesus-chuy-garcia-reelection-dropping-out-chief-of-staff-running" target="_blank" >The last-minute maneuver</a> — within an hour of the deadline — ensured Rep. García could bow out of the race and Patty García, no relation, could run in his place. Rep. García later said he was stepping down due to health and family reasons, but it left Patty García as the only Democrat on the ballot, almost assuring her of winning the traditionally blue seat. </p><p>In announcing her run in November, she defended that process, saying any other Democrat could have jumped into the race before Rep. García opted out. </p><p>“It’s an open process. Any person who’s interested in running for office can apply, can circulate their petitions and submit an application. We followed the rules. We collected signatures, and we submitted an application,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2025/11/12/patty-garcia-chuy-congress-ballot-chicago-march-primary" target="_blank" >she said during her first campaign appearance</a> at a grocery store in her hometown of Cicero. “People can apply at any point. We didn’t stop anybody from applying.”</p><p>Her name was also thrown around in constant criticisms coming from independent challengers Ald. Byron Sigcho-Lopez and Mayra Macías, who were both told on Tuesday by the Illinois State Board of Elections that they <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/07/21/byron-sigcho-lopez-mayra-macias-chuy-garcia-congressional-seat-independent-candidates-ballot-removal" target="_blank" >did not submit enough valid nominating petitions</a> to make it onto the ballot as independent candidates. Both have said Patty García and Rep. García's decision left voters without choices. Sigcho-Lopez has said he's reviewing legal options, and Macías is considering a write-in campaign. But Patty García said she's not worried about those challenges.</p><p>"What I'm worried about right now is making sure that we can get to to voters... For me, it's making sure that we get to as many voters as possible to let them know why this race matters to them, and why I'm the most viable candidate and someone who has been doing the work and can best represent this district," Patty García said. "That's what I'm focused on. Making sure that we can win in November and take back the House."</p><p>Patty García is now backed by a coalition of unions, community organizations and elected leaders, including U.S. Reps. García and Delia Ramirez, Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Juliana Stratton, Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias and Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle. Union support is coming from the Illinois AFL-CIO, Our Revolution, Chicago Federation of Labor and the SEIU Illinois State Council. Her campaign has also raised more than $350,000.</p><p>Little Village resident Lupe Castillo is running for the Republican nomination, and Bridgeport resident Ed Hershey is running as a candidate of the Working Class Party. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/05/23/independent-challengers-sigcho-lopez-macias-getty-patty-garcia-chuy-garcia-seat" target="_blank" >Lyons Mayor Chris Getty is the sole independent candidate</a> after Tuesday's State Board of Elections hearing. Objectors didn't file a challenge against Getty's petitions.</p>
entries.author: Tina Sfondeles
